I beg to lay on the table

St. Lawrence Waterway

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I quite appreciate the statement made by the right hon. the Prime Minister with respect to this matter, but I cannot but think that having regard to the circumstances that must have been present in his mind he might have tabled the documents at six o'clock before the house rose, for the press had them in their possession since the morning, although not to be used until later, as I understood at midnight; and the members of parliament might have been entrusted with the same documents at six o'clock or at eight o'clock at any rate. It is true the house adjourned rather earlier than was expected, but on the other hand the Prime Minister knew of his engagement and I am sure that if he had intimated that he would be absent from the house, they could have been laid on the table by one of his ministers at eight o'clock. I cannot think it is using parliament quite right to have these documents published in the newspapers and widely known to a very considerable number of people before we have any knowledge of them at all. I hardly think that is consistent with the dignity of the house. I do not, however, for a moment think that the Prime Minister wittingly adopted that method of dealing with documents intended for the information of the house.
The motion with respect to the printing of the documents enables me to say something further in connection with another matter of the same kind. Not long since, a document was published in a Toronto paper before it became known at all to the members of this house. I understand that the explanation of it is that the commissioner who made the report gave a copy of it to the newspaper thereby enabling it to be printed. That is, it seems to me, a very reprehensible practice and one that this house should not at all sanction. A report that is to be laid upon the table of the house should not be given to the newspapers until such time as it has been tabled. The adoption of a contrary course is really an insult to members of parliament. I investigated this matter at the time, and my information led me to conclude that the government was not to blame, but rather the commissioner who made the report. I think that principle is quite wrong. Certainly members of parliament should enjoy as much latitude in connection with matters of this kind as the press of the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I say
that I agree entirely with my hon. friend in all that he has said as to the procedure which should be followed, but I think the house will
see in a moment that it was a pure accident that hon. members did not receive these documents last night as was anticipated. In the first place as to the press having copies of the correspondence, my hon. friend knows that with respect to important documents of any length it is sometimes the practice to give copies in advance to the press on the undertaking that they will not be released until a certain time. In connection with the correspondence between the United States and Canada on the St. Lawrence waterway project the understanding was that the press in both countries should receive the documents on Monday at the latest, and the Canadian Press on Saturday night, but that the press summaries of the documents were only to be released for Tuesday morning's papers-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: After midnight.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the purpose being to enable the Canadian Press and the Associated Press to send full despatches and obviate the necessity of individual correspondents telegraphing lengthy communications to their respective papers. It was intimated to me by members of the press gallery that in the case of these papers it would not be advisable to confine the copies that were being given out to the Canadian Press, but that they should be given to all the members of the gallery on the understanding that they would not be released in any case until after the adjournment of the house on Monday night. This was agreed to and I have every reason to believe that the members of the press in that particular have kept faith with the government.
As to tabling	the	papers	at	six	o'clock, Imay say to my	hon.	friend	that I	had themin my desk and the thought entered my mind to table them at the hour mentioned when I recalled a conversation I had had with respect to the hour of tabling and mention of the- fact that what would be regarded as an early hour here was still earlier in some parts of the western states and western Canada, and that it	would	be	breaking faithwith others to	allow any	of	the	afternoon
papers to receive in advance any intimation at all of what was in the documents. Therefore I deliberately refrained from carrying out the thought I had at the moment of tabling the papers at six o'clock.
Now as to the events of the evening, I fully expected to be in the house not later than half-past nine. As a matter of fact I was in the house by twenty minutes of ten. In the interval, however, the house had adjourned and I had no alternative but to defer tabling the papers until to-day.
Federal District Commission

I should like to ask the. Prime Minister a question. Could he not have intrusted the leader of the opposition and the leader of hon. members to the left of Mr. Speaker with copies of the correspondence on the same terms as in the case of the press?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should have been very happy to do so, had I thought my hon. friend might have wished to have the documents in advance. Another time I shall perhaps profit by this experience and see that he gets them a little in advance. As a matter of fact the documents were in my desk in the house and had it been anticipated that adjournment was to take place when it did some of my colleagues might readily have opened the desk and tabled the papers before the house adjourned. I think however everyone now has full information in the form in which it will be found most accessible.

Will an opportunity be
given to resume the adjourned debate on this question?

speechtext: The house resumed, from April 13, consideration in committee of Bill No. 199, to amend the Dominion Lands Act.-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton) Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this bill was last before the committee certain progress had been made. Section 1 had been struck out. The committee were considering what appears as section 2 in the bill and which will now become section 1.
On section 2-Second homestead.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I move to amend this clause in the thirteenth line by changing the figure "8" to the figure "5", and by striking from

Dominion Lands Act
the fourteenth and fifteenth lines the words "in the discretion of the minister". The clause will then read:
Provided, however, that any person who on the first day of January, 1925, had obtained or had become entitled to letters patent for a homestead as aforesaid, may be granted the right to make entry for a second homestead, subject to the provisions of this act.

I would like to know
why the change has been made to 1925. If a man is entitled to a second homestead who has become entitled to letters patent for his homestead before January 1, 1925, why should not that apply to the man who has become entitled to letters patent in 1926, 1927 or 1928?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The criticism of the clause as it was originally drafted was that it would give rise to speculation, although frankly I do not agree very much with that criticism. At all events, this provides for a longer interval between the dates on which a man has proved up and received letters patent for his homestead and the date upon which he may make application for his second homestead. It may tend to prevent an individual proving up and then at once selling his homestead and making application for a second one. On the whole, I think the precaution is a wise one.

Does this provision apply to
the whole of the western provinces or only to the dry area?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: To the whole of the western provinces.

When this scheme was first
projected, it was with the idea of giving a chance to those homesteaders who had failed to establish themselves in the dry parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta particularly. When we were called into conference last year at Regina, some of us understood that that was the purpose of the whole scheme. I must say now, as I said then, that I am opposed to giving a second homestead indiscriminately to all who may feel disposed to apply for it. It is going to upset tremendously conditions throughout western Canada. It will mean more vacant homesteads; the weed crop itself will be a considerable trial to the municipalities, and speculation and other factors will enter in so that conditions will not be improved by giving the second homestead indiscriminately to all who wish to apply for it. I would confine the application of this act to those who have settled in the dry areas and failed to establish themselves as they expected.

Does this apply to the
Peace River country and the land in the railway belt of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, just to the crown lands open for homesteading.

There are crown lands
open for homesteading in the Peace River country, are there not?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In the
Peace River block, yes, but not very many of them.

And in the railway belt
also.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Not in the
railway belt.
Oh yes. I think the minister is mistaken. There are pre-emptions granted in the railway belt.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That is
different.

I wish to say a few words in support of this measure. It is true, as the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) says, that when we gathered in Regina to discuss this matter, he took the attitude there that he takes here to-day, but some others of us voiced the opinion that this was good legislation for various reasons. I know that in the particular district from which I come we have been homesteading for some twenty years, and we find there many good Canadians who have come in from other parts of Canada, particularly from Ontario, and immigrants from overseas. We find families who settled in that district eighteen and twenty years ago, with four or five of a family. Some of those families to-day have two or three boys who are in a position to take up a homestead, and who under the existing law could take up a homestead, but they do not wish to leave the family roof, and if the father can be given the opportunity of taking up a second homestead, it will keep the family united. I believe that that is a good thing, and from my own experience in homesteading I believe that those people who have already had experience in homesteading will be an asset to any new country that is being opened up. As conditions are to-day, these people cannot extend their activities in the district where they are already located because of the high price of land, and the result is that the boys are drifting into the towns and cities, but when the father is given the opportunity of taking up a second homestead, a privilege which I think should be granted, the boys will
Dominion Lands Act

come back home and probably homestead again. I am heartily in support of this particular section.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Terms of payment.

Has the minister any intention of restricting the provision of this act to the dried out area? The constituency of Willow Bunch which I represent has been considered wholly in this dried out area, and we feel that that is a black eye for the district. We have been farming in there for the last fifteen or twenty years, and we have had crops every year, and we feel that we should not be dubbed as a dried out area. We think the definition of this dried out area should be limited in some way. All through that district we find many returned soldiers living in the towns and unaible to get homesteads because they have no land within the nine miles, and they have to fake either the sale or renting of land before they can file on land. Last fall we opened up a lease in that district, and some of the returned soldiers went in there and faked sales and leases of land to allow them to file on this land. We have farm labourers who have come into that district and worked there for four or five years, living with the farmer, and they cannot go out and take up a homestead, but the farmer's son can. They have to buy or lease land before they can enter on land for a homestead. There are some districts in southern Alberta where probably this might apply, but we do not think it does apply to the constituency which I have the honour to represent. We think this should be restricted.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
When the
bill was in committee on a previous occasion the criticism was that the legislation had worked out very well, but that it would be unwise to widen its scope and throw all this territory south of township 31 in Saskatchewan and Alberta open for homesteading. I suggested that the amendment proposed be stricken out. I may say that I agree entirely with the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly). This summer I shall arrange in conjunction with the provincial government and their officials to make a close inspection of the territory mentioned by him and several other hon. members who represent constituencies in southern Saskatchewan, and next session I hope to submit an amendment that will provide for definite sections to be thrown open for homesteading generally.
I Mr. Variance.]

From the remarks of the hon. minister I assume that there is no immediate intention to turn over to the provinces their natural resources. With respect to the terms of payment on school lands, as amended by section 4, I do not think the amendment goes far enough to meet the situation in Alberta. I have a return before me showing that at a sale of school lands last fall one Joseph S. McCallum purchased 3,739 acres, and another A. Shandro, purchased 19,677 acres. I think it may be taken for granted that neither one of those purchasers intends to farm the land so acquired. In all probability they found certain farmers were interested in purchasing, and then said, "All right>
you give us a dollar an acre and we will buy the land." I know one man replied that he was quite competent to buy the land himself, and thereupon those speculators ran the particular quarter-section up to $60 an acre, although generally speaking it would not be worth more than $10 or $12 an acre. That was the policy followed all through the recent sales of school lands: unless the farmers gave them a commission to make the purchase they ran up the price ridiculously high. I think it is the intention of those men not to make any further payments unless they can resell the land at a profit; otherwise they are prepared to lose their first payment. It is simply a case of speculation. I think the minister should so amend the act that no one purchaser would be able to secure more than a quarter or a half-section of land.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend may remember that some ten years ago W. J. McNamara purchased a large quantity of school lands along the right of way of the then Canadian Northern Railway system in northern Alberta. I felt this was an injustice to the people generally, and I spent two or three days down here with the then Minister of the Interior in an attempt to devise ways and means to prevent the recurrence of such a case. But we were met with this very practical difficulty, that all government officials have discovered that the fairest way in which to dispose of school lands is to offer them for sale at public auction. This results in better prices being obtained for the land and provides the most efficient means against fraud that has yet been devised. Of course, it does not prevent an individual from acquiring more land than he intends to farm, but it does have just the effect my hon. friend has mentioned, where a group of farmers get together and arrange not to bid more than a certain amount for any quarter-section. However, that is not the evil that I am trying

Dominion Lands Act
to cure by this bill. My primary purpose is to get a sufficient first payment. We have discovered that one-twentieth is too small an investment on the part of the purchaser to warrant his holding the land if it does not suit his convenience, with the result that he abandons it in very bad condition. I think to dispose of these lands at public auction without any particular restrictions is the best method that can be devised for attaining fair and reasonable prices and thus getting the largest return for the school fund-the object for which the land is set aside.
What is the usual term after the initial payment has been made?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Twenty
years.

When was the term
changed from ten to twenty years?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The change was made by me some three or four years ago.

I do not agree with the Minister of the Interior; I think the terms have been absolutely too lax, with the result that many of our western farmers have gambled in school lands. This change from one-twentieth to one-tenth is a step in the right direction, but still the terms of sale are too easy. The trouble is that a man will buy school lands and not complete his payments, farming them for ten or fourteen years. If the department presses him very hard he will rent the land at fifty cents an acre and continue farming for another ten or fifteen years.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: He can only rent the land pending another sale.

The terms are far too easy. The purchaser should be made to pay in two or three years, just as he would be obliged to do if he had bought from a private individual. If he fails to make his payments the land should be put up at auction and rented at a certain percentage of the upset value. For example, if it was worth $25 an acre, make the rent 8 per cent on that value. Either do that or call for tenders. Many farmers will bid up land to $50, $60 and $75 an acre, and I have seen them bid as high as $80 an acre, with no intention whatever of buying it. They bid it in to control it for the next eight or ten years. He puts up one-twentieth and then sits back and in four, eight or ten years' time he throws it back on the government. He rents the land at fifty cents an acre, and neighbouring farmers who want to rent it cannot do so. This man continues to hold the land at fifty cents until the government puts it up at auction and then 56103-133
he bids it in again paying one-twentieth or one-tenth, and continues ownership. That has been done time and time again in the district I represent. Last summer in two or three sales I saw land run up 50 per cent more than the land was worth in what was nothing but a fake sale, for that land was not sold. The only object is that these individuals may hold the land in this way. Unless we become more strict in our sales we shall not be able to sell our school lands, and they will become polluted with weeds, dirt and so forth, so that they will be worth little or nothing. It seems to me the time has come when we should take measures to enforce more severe terms in connection with these school lands.

I wish to support what
the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has said. Two or three years ago I was informed that the money owing on school lands in Saskatchewan and Alberta amounted to some $3,000,000. As the hon. member (Mr. Donnelly) has said, there are school lands-I know of many cases-where the price was run up to a fair amount and only the first payment was made. That is going on all the time. There are people who hold lands for eight and ten years without paying anything more than the first instalment. In the interests of the country we should in my opinion, be more severe. It is only reasonable, where climatic conditions adverse to agriculture warrant it, to afford the buyers fair opportunity to come through. But where crops are obtained on these lands the department should be more strict than it is at the present time.

Most of the difficulties
I have observed in connection with school, Indian and other government lands in my constituency have been due to the manipulations of speculators and' not to anything on the part of bona fide farmers. We find a condition out there such as the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner) has referred to. A group of speculators will attend sales, and at the particular season of year farmers anxious to obtain lands may not have any money with which to purchase them. The result is that a speculator gets the land cheap; or perhaps a group of them will combine so as to eliminate opposition, and then by the time the regular farmer, the man who really intends to till the soil, to break up the land and make a farm out of it, is ready and anxious to get hold of the land, he finds that the price has gone up $5, $10 and in some cases $15 and $20 per acre. Then what

Dominion Lands Act

does the speculator do? He collects year after year all he can obtain from the farmer without turning one dollar in to the department. If the minister will look over the books in the school lands branch as well as in the other branches to which I have alluded, he will find case after case where land was sold to some speculator, a man who never was a farmer and never intended to farm, and then resold to bona fide farmers at greatly enhanced prices. His game is to withhold the money from the department, and in the cases in which I have had to make representations to the minister's department I have discovered that lands have been held five, six, and in some cases, ten and twelve years. During all this time the farmers have been making regular payments to the speculators while the department has not secured a dollar. I have been able to get the departmental officers in many instances to cancel their undertaking with the speculators and to re-lease to bona fide farmers, with the hope of ultimately selling to them when they are in a position to buy. If we are to avoid trouble of this kind in the future the proper thing for us to do is to compel the purchaser to effect improvements on the land. I would not go so far as to compel him to reside on it because the owner might be a farmer living on his own adjoining farm, But if the department is to avoid a lot of these difficulties in the future and at the same time be just to those who are tilling the soil it would be in the interests of these people as well as to the advantage of the government to impose some specific obligations upon the purchaser in connection with the land. Those difficulties of which I have knowledge in my own district have arisen for the most part in connection with Indian lands, and there are some very sad cases in this regard, where farmers have paid in $1,500, $1,800 and sometimes, $2,000 or more to the speculator, believing all the time that he was keeping up his payments to the department, and after a lapse of ten years he finds to his amazement that not a dollar has been paid by the speculator apart from the initial instalment. Then he is threatened with cancellation. In some cases the cancellation proceedings deprive the farmer of the land which he has been farming. But the speculator has secured his profit and he is not very greatly concerned. I agree with the minister on the reasons he has given for raising the initial payment from one-twentieth to one-tenth. That decision, I think, is sound. I think, however, the minister would relieve his officers of a good deal of trouble, and at the same
IMr. Campbell.]
time do justice to the farmers, if by legislation he compelled the purchaser to carry out certain improvements on the land within a specified time.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
A serious
difficulty suggests itself in connection with the point raised by my hon. friend. In connection with both school and Indian lands we find a good many farmers entering into agreements of sale with people who owe the government money, and never taking the precaution to notify us that the sale has taken place. We know nothing about the matter and we continue notifying the purchaser year after year. We make annual demands for payment and we receive what appear to be reasonable excuses for non-payment. No doubt in a few cases hardship is entailed where payments have been made to the purchaser while no return is made to the department; and this notwithstanding the fact that \Ve have sent out warnings pointing out the importance of our being notified. While we do not intend to be harsh in the collection of these outstanding accounts, I think the purchasers of these lands will realize from now on that we are going to be more insistent than ever that the obligations to the government shall be lived up to in connection with school lands and Indian lands as well. We have had a good deal of difficulty. Times have been bad and we have been somewhat patient, but there does not appear to be any good reason why we should not receive substantial payments and have a clearance of these outstanding obligation within a reasonable time.

What is the effect of these words in subsection 4:
Provided that the government of the province in which the land is situated expresses its approval of the sale and price in each case.
Does that mean that the government of the province in which the land is situate must consent to and approve the terms of the sale?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No. It is
by agreement with the province that the sales take place, and by agreement with the province that the interest charges are fixed. With the single exception of the date of sale, the provinces are consulted about all school lands.
But it says "in each sale."

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That is
necessary in order to cover the situation.

I submit to the minister that the most important factor of the sale i3

Dominion Lands Act
not getting a big price for these lands. I think the upset price which is put on the land is the fairer price, and it would be better for the country generally if the land were sold at that price than at a higher rate. Perhaps the minister will remember when the Saddle Lake reserve lands were sold; a large tract of land was sold to two or three buyers, but the department cancelled the sale and later sold the land again. At the later sale no individual was allowed to purchase more than a half-section, and I do not see why a similar clause could not be introduced in this legislation.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The case is not parallel at all, because a portion of the Saddle Lake reserve was turned over to the soldier settlement board at a fixed rate of $10 per acre, if I remember correctly. They were unable to settle that land, and a portion of it was turned over for local settlement at the same price and with the same adjustment. The only provision we made was to prevent speculation, because the price was fixed, and we intended to prevent any individual from securing an undue portion of the reserve.

I think the minister
should take into consideration the suggestion made by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell).

With reference
to this matter of speculation, it is true that ten years ago there was a good deal of speculation in school lands, for several reasons. One reason was that the land could be secured by a comparatively small initial payment, and the price of grain was exceedingly high. When wheat was worth over $2 per bushel and oats sold for more than $1 per bushel, many men bought land at ridiculously high prices, expecting the high prices for grain to continue. Eight years ago this coming summer oats sold for SI .25 per bushel in the district to which the hon. member for Mackenzie referred, and at that price certainly land would be worth S100 per acre. Men went out and bought land at prices up to S70 per acre before the slump came in the fall; then oats dropped to about one-half the former price, and by the following summer oats of the same quality were selling for about 35 cents per bushel at the same point. If the department had stepped in then and dealt harshly with the people who had bought land, many of whom were not speculators but real farmers extending their holdings, there would have been a great deal of suffering caused and the 5 per cent of the purchase price which had been paid would 56103-133J
have been lost. That situation has been more or less cleaned up in the intervening years; agriculture has become more prosperous, and now is the time to guard against the recurrence of those conditions. The people throughout the western country are looking for an opportunity 'to buy school lands; the sale which was held last year indicated that there was a good demand even for land which was not new and which was not as clean in many cases as it might have been. There is a pretty good demand to-day from many legitimate farmers for this land, and I think this provision under which we will collect 10 per cent of the purchase price instead of 5 per cent will check careless speculating.
The example quoted by the hon. member for Athabaska a few moments ago is something which very rarely happens. Land worth $10 per acre was run up to $60, and of that sum 5 per cent was paid. That payment amounted to $3 or 35 per cent of its real value. The speculator could not run up the price of that land by himself; he had to have competition, and a real farmer does not often run up land to a ridiculously high price, although he will run it up to what it is worth to him because of its proximity to his own holdings. In this case apparently the department already has received 35 per cent of the value of the land, and if this amendment had been in force at that time the department would have collected for the school fund 60 per cent of its real value. In these cases there are two parties to the procedure; first, we have the real owners of these lands, and it is incumbent upon the minister to secure every dollar he can possibly get from these lands for the provincial school funds. At the same time what the hon. member for Athabaska has said must be borne in mind; it is better to sell these lands as nearly as possible at their actual value, because then it is more likely that they will be paid for.
Then just a word about improvements; that is a very loose term, and may include a great deal or very little. The hon. member for Mackenzie does not want to see a man forced to live on the land because that might interfere with his residence elsewhere, and I quite agree with him. But when he asks that the department should request the man to carry on other improvements I cannot agree, because I imagine he means breaking and cultivating the land, and in many cases that is the worst thing that can happen. It would not be a good thing to compel a speculator to cultivate land; the legitimate farmer is going to cultivate his land as quickly as possible, because there is no revenue from it
Dominion Lands Act

while it is idle, but to take steps which would force the speculator to cultivate the land himself would not be good business because in most cases it would become polluted with weeds and would have to be taken in and sold again if the speculator fell down in his payments. If that were done it would not be worth as much as it was worth before anything was done to it. There is a remedy for that condition, which has been working satisfactorily during the last few years. There is no doubt that the wild lands tax which is collected from such vacant lands in the western provinces has compelled large holders of land to either sell their land to someone who will cultivate it or to cultivate and improve it themselves in such a way as to enable them to avoid paying that tax.
I think this amendment raising to 10 per cent the deposit paid in the first instance is a good thing, and at this time, when demands for land are becoming more general, it will help avoid such speculation as we have had. The balance of the question can be handled by administration; this is a good time to tighten up on collections, because as we know any one who suggested in this house or in the country five or six years ago that we should tighten up on collections would not have been very popular, because it was hard for farmers to get along without paying anything on the capital cost of their land.

After listening to this
discussion I think there is a keen desire on the part of the committee to restrict the sale of school lands to bona fide farmers who can buy and pay for them. It has been suggested that by raising the initial payment we will keep out the speculator, but I have spoken to a speculator in land within the last few days who told me that that is not so, that the higher the initial payment is made the greater his chance will be. I quite believe that to a certain extent, because many of the western farmers to-day in those districts where school lands are available are not able to make a very high initial payment. However, we may have this condition; one man may buy school land for $10 an acre, while another man pays from $50 to $60 for similar land. They both fall down on their contracts, appeal to the department, sign a quit claim deed, and then obtain the privilege of renting that land for 50 cents per acre. If in the one instance the land was only worth $10 per acre while the other land was worth $60, surely the privilege of renting the land is w'orth more to the man who had the $60 land than to the man who had the $10 land. The higher price paid for certain land would indicate that the pro-

ductive power of that land is greater, and therefore I think there ought to be a further tightening up of the regulations. I am absolutely with the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) in the statement that the land should be put in a condition where the farmer who is to cultivate it can do so as easily as possible.

We have certainly fallen
somewhat on evil times in certain parts of the west during the last few years. With the exception of those in Alberta our people out there have not recovered from the years 1918, 1919, 1920 and perhaps will not for some time to come. I do not wish to see conditions made much harder for those people who are trying to establish themselves in certain districts where the rain-fall is rather scarce. Another thing, I am of opinion that this legislation is very untimely at this stage. Is there such urgency for the sale of school lands that on the very eve of the handing over of their natural resources to the prairie provinces the government feels impelled to pass a measure of this kind? What urgent need is there of this legislation? Does the minister think there is going to be a large sale of school land?	If not what is the
reason for this urgency? I think the whole thing is untimely and might just as well be deferred seeing that we are on the eve of giving to the prairie provinces their natural resources.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend may I say that while there is every hope their natural resources will be transferred to the provinces the transfer has not yet been effected, and I am sure he would be the last one to suggest that the whole machinery under which those resources are operated should stop. May I assure him that no arrangement of this kind is made without the consent of the provincial governments or discussion with them with only one single exception and that is the plan alluded to with respect to the renting of the land. It is the intention to apply these amendments to lands that fall back on our hands where failure to make payment is made and the purchaser is closed out, and where we may have for one year, or two at the most, the land under lease. Because it is the most unsatisfactory business we have to deal with in connection with the sale of school lands. We much prefer to deal with purchasers rather than with tenants. We have had a great deal of difficulty in that regard. It is not our intention to allow tenancy to continue for more than two years but there will be a public sale of the lands and new purchasers will be sought for them. In the matter of the

Dominion Lands Act
short period that may intervene before there is a resale of the land, and other amendments also, we have been in consultation with the provincial governments concerned.

Has the department any rules by which the buyers of school lands are allowed to keep on with their payments without those lands being put up for resale? i
jfc. .

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: After consultation with the provincial governments it was decided not to execute the sale of the school lands, but I may say that I pressed upon them the desirability of allowing the sale of improved lands that were held under lease to go on in order to avoid the difficulties encountered in leasing these lands. So far as I know they are all sold at the present time, but reversions are always taking place. We have to take measures to prevent the lands growing weeds and the obvious thing to do is to lease them for a short period. I trust that period will be very short indeed in future.

Have the provincial governments asked for this particular legislation?
M,r. STEWART (Edmonton): Yes.
What I wanted to find out was for how many years can a buyer continue to farm a piece of land after he has made only one payment or before his ownership is cancelled?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Unless he
suffers an absolute failure of crop we expect a payment every year. That has not been the case. I am free to admit we have been somewhat lenient during the bad years settlers have recently passed through. Now we are making more careful inspection, and where we know the purchaser has had a reasonable crop and should be in a position to make payment, we intend to press very strenuously for payment.

Is there any intention
to change the terms of the lease?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I tried to
make it clear to the committee that it is not our intention to continue leasing. Just as soon as it can possibly be done we will resell the land.

I wanted to know
whether you intend changing the terms of the lease?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is not our intention to do so. We have a very simple method. It is easy of administration and it does not require inspection.
Mr. FAN3HER (Last Mountain):	What
objection would the minister have to stipulating that not more than one half-section could be purchased by any single individual? This would prevent operations by speculators and would give a bona fide farmer a much better chance of acquiring a holding if he desired to do 60.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
If in any
given locality you restrict the purchase to a quarter or half-section, you immediately have collusion amongst the purchasers in the locality and the price will be depressed to that extent. We have found by experience that the easiest method is to allow free competition. I think there is no doubt that the school land fund has profited proportionately by the free competition which prevails in connection with the purchase of these lands, notwithstanding the fact that in some cases the prices of lands do go to unprecedented heights. I want to say that in many cases where high prices are paid we have not the same amount of difficulty in collection, and the reason that I am making the change back to the one-tenth payment down is that most of our difficulty arises from the fact that the actual individual on ordinary priced land, not on land purchased at too high a figure, appears to have good and sufficient reason for delay in making his payments, with the result that he falls into serious arrears.
May I say a word with respect to the improvements? These matters have all been discussed with the provincial governments who are extremely anxious to get the best prices possible, because, as I pointed out a moment or two ago, they are the ones who benefit by these prices. The better the prices are. the more money they have for their school land funds. While one can, find many criticisms to offer, after years of experience these are the methods that have been adopted. I am not averse at all and will agree this year, if we continue to administer these lands, to discussing with the provincial governments the advisability of asking for improvements during the first or second year of purchase; but until I have an opportunity of discussing this matter with them, I do not care to embody such a provision in the legislation.

I do not object to the
proposal of the minister to ask for an initial payment of one-tenth; but in view of the remarks which have been made by some members of the committee, I should like to suggest that, after a piece of school land has been purchased and several payments made upon it, the department should not be very
Dominion Lands Act

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: strict in enforcing payment of the principal, because the unpaid principal as soon as it falls into arrears is drawing seven per cent interest. The minister himself stated that it was the desire of the provinces to get as much money as possible out of these school lands. Once the principal is paid it is impossible for the government to secure a rate of seven per cent interest on it. In some cases I have made representations to the department on behalf of parties who were in arrears on their contracts, but who were keeping their interest paid up. As long as they are paying the interest, and particularly such a handsome rate as seven per cent, I think the department should not press these people for payment of the principal provided they are keeping the farm in good shape. It is good business for the provinces to have this rate of interest coming in.

I quite agree with the minister that a sale free from all restrictions may make a better showing on the date of sale; that is, the amount realized at the date of sale might be a little larger than if certain restrictions such as I suggested were attached to the sale, but that does not mean that the government will ultimately secure that amount for the land. The reason I make that suggestion to the minister is that the sales will be good sales. The minister himself knows, and the records of his department will show that scores of these sales are not sales at all. Some speculator secures the land, turns it over to a farmer and expects the farmer to pay up the balance. The speculator collects all he can from the farmer; he stands the department off. and years after, when he has extracted a large amount from the farmer and got his money out of the land, he drops out of the picture altogether. In this way many cases of hardship arise as regards the department as well as the ultimate purchaser, and I think that should be avoided.
In that particular case you might have a very satisfactory showing on the date of the sale but it would not be very satisfactory ultimately to the department. Many of those sales, as I think the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) intimated, were made at a time when land prices were unduly inflated, and just because during a long period these speculators were standing the department off. little or nothing was collected. Now that land is in many cases back on the hands of the department and it must be sold for probably less than half the price it was sold for at that time. My point is that had that land been purchased originally with certain improvement conditions attached to the sale,
fMr. Coot.tf.1
it perhaps would not have sold at as high a price, but in most cases the department would have secured more money than they did on sales made without restriction. I still think the minister would be well advised to insert some such restriction as that in the statute.

The minister stated a
fete- minutes ago that he was afraid there might be collusion among the parties. Unquestionably there has been collusion under these regulations, and as regards getting into trouble, I think the minister is in trouble at present. Let us take, for instance, the case that I cited a moment ago of A. Shandro who purchased 123 quarter-sections. I am satisfied he is well known to the minister and I think the minister will admit that unless he sells that land again, it will never be paid for. The only way Shandro can pay for that land is by re-selling it, and I cannot for the life of me see the object in getting him to purchase a large quantity of land like that simply to make some bona fide farmer pay him a commission. The man does not intend to farm and he has no immediate prospect of re-selling the land. He will make his first payment; he will hang on until he runs across some farmer who wants to buy it, and he will then make that farmer pay him a commission. That is not good business for the government of this country to follow and I want even yet to endeavour to persuade the minister to add to this legislation a clause which will limit sales to at most half a section to any one person.

While I agree with the
hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner), who is trying to limit to a certain extent the purchase of land under the School Lands Act,
I would not limit it to quite such a small quantity as half a section. I think we should put a limit on people buying 25', 50, 75 or 100 quarter-sections. I take it that the main object in selling this land is to get more settlers, but sales made in this way are purely a matter of speculation.
I wish to say a few words with regard to the statement made by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). There is something in what he says about not pressing the farmer too hard if the interest payments have been kept up; but my main criticism is that there are too many purchasers of land who are not keeping up their payments of either principal or interest, and in. those cases I think the department should be a great deal stricter than it is. Where they are not paying either interest or principal, their right to the land,

Dominion Lands Act
should be cancelled at an early date unless they are suffering from difficult climatic conditions.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I shall be
very glad to bring all these representations to the attention of the provincial governments; but inasmuch as this is being done by agreement between the Department of the Interior and the provincial governments, I do not care this year to add to or take from the amendment anything that will materially affect it.
I shall, however, be glad to bring before the provincial government the question of the restriction of individual purchases, although I say very frankly that I shall not advocate it;
I will oppose it, because I think the effect will be exactly the reverse of what my hon. friends expect. I think free and unrestricted sale is the best method of getting the most money out of these' lands. If an individual takes his chance on paying one-twentieth down on each quarter-section that he purchases, he is taking a chance on re-selling or on our closing him out if he is holding these lands for purely speculative purposes. That has not been done in the past, I am free to admit. I have in mind particularly those lands along the old Canadian Northern railway. It is not the intention to allow speculators to hold lands indefinitely out of use. They usually do not do so; usually these lands are leased for grazing purposes; but our difficulty starts when we have an individual farming the land and failing to make payments so that finally we have to close him out. In that case we have the cultivated lands on our hands, and if we do not do something with them they grow up with weeds and we are bombarded by the municipalities to clean them up. That is where our difficulty starts. However, I will make the best presentation possible of all these suggestions to the provincial governments and be prepared, if we are in control, to embody them in amendments next year.

I do not agree with the minister at all on one point, and it seems to be his chief ground for rejecting now, and expressing his intention of rejecting in the future, the suggestion that has been made by the hon. member for Athabasca. What is the minister going to do with a situation like this? Up in the district of Mundare, we will say, there are school lands to be sold. The people in the district of Mundare, many of them, do not speak English fluently, although a few of them do, of course. Some of them want to buy a piece of these school lands, and a gentleman of a certain delicate type of occupation learns that
there is to be a sale of these school lands, and he goes down amongst these people and says, "You are going to be up against a difficult proposition. Just leave it all to me. You do not need to appear at the sale at all.
I will buy the land for you and look after everything." He makes himself a good fellow, and for a commission proceeds to make the purchase. He buys the land from the department at a lower price than the land- would have brought had he not called off all these people. He will have an agreement with several of these people to get this one a certain piece of land, and that one a certain other piece. There is collusion of the worst type in the open auction sale method, because as soon as that agent has bought the land he goes back to these poor individuals for whom he has purchased it, and in addition to the commission he intends charging, he adds something to the purchase price of the land, and they have no way of dealing with him; they have simply to pay him his price, because the sale is made to him in the first place by the department. It has been called to my attention that many cases of that kind have occurred during the last year in the northern districts where school land sales have taken place. I do not know just how the minister is going to cope with that situation. I think the ideal solution would be to say that no land shall be sold to anyone who is not a bona fide farmer, but the difficulty there is to define a bona fide farmer accurately for the purpose of the act. In the face of that difficulty I think the minister should really take into his sympathetic consideration the proposal of the hon. member for Athabaska, especially in view of the fact that, in spite of the words of the hon. member for Melfort, there is no doubt in my mind but that if the prosperous conditions which my hon. friends opposite so loudly declare exist now in western Canada and elsewhere continue, then inevitably there is going to be a steadily upward trend in the price of land. These men know it. I feel myself that such will be the case, and if conditions in the west are going to be better, and I believe they are getting better now, there is going to be as wide speculation as possible.
I agree with the hon. member for South Battleford that the increase in the initial payment is not going to stop the speculator, but it will stop the farmer who has not much cash in the bank, but has a couple of growing sons for whom he would like to hold a certain piece of land. He has not the money to put up, but Mr. Doctor or Mr. Lawyer or Mr. Somebody else in the nearby town sees there a fine chance for himself. He has the capital,

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not
say so.

Nor do I
think it will put the land under cultivation any sooner. Under the old system, if the payment was smaller at the start, there would be more chance of the farmer getting the land and bringing it under cultivation. Frankly, I do not think the minister has made much of a job of these changes, and if the provincial governments have agreed to them, then all I have to say is that perhaps some of them need revision themselves, and some of them quite clearly do.
I think the best point that has been raised so far was raised by the hon. member for Mackenzie and by the hon. member for Athabaska. In my opinion in connection with all these sales of land the attempt should be to get them into the hands of bona fide farmers and bring them under cultivation as soon as possible, and you can best do that, first, by providing that the improvements must be done. They will not always do them, but that provision would help. Secondly, prevent the sale of large blocks of land to any single individual, not more than a section to any individual.

I think it would be good
policy for this government and for the provincial governments interested to say that not more than four quarter-sections of school lands shall be sold to any one man at any of these sales. I know of cases where speculators have bought as much as thirty quarters at a school lands sale, and then have sold that land to the farmers who lived near at an advance in price. It would take the farmer four or five years to pay off the increased value which the speculator had put on the land, and for years the farmer would not be able to pay anything to the department. The department kindly allows them to hold this land without paying interest, let alone principal, and after the farmer has taken four or five years to pay off the increased value which the speculator charges him, he then begins to pay off the department. I think the land would bring just as much if it was sold with a limit of four quarter-sections to any one man, and certainly it would cut out a lot of the speculation that now goes on. The
[Air. E. J. Garland.]
provinces will admit that it is to their interest to get this land under cultivation as soon as possible, as well as to get a good price for the land, and any loss the provinces might suffer by limiting sales to four quarter-sections to any one individual would easily be offset by the less amount of speculation which would take place and by having the land brought under cultivation sooner.

Mr. Chairman, when the house rose at six o'clock last night doubt was expressed by my hon. friends opposite regarding the words, " most-favoured-nation ", some contending that their inclusion would give Czechoslovakia the advantages of our tariff arrangements with the mother country. To make sure of our position. I then wired to the representatives of The Netherlands and this is the reply I received:
I have tile honour to inform you that according to a cable dated May 20,'received from the Minister of Foreign Affairs at The Hague, The Netherlands government has not at all the intention to claim the benefits of the said British preferential tariff under article one of said Canadian-Netherlands convention; and furthermore, that in the opinion of The Netherlands government the claiming of the benefits of the said British preferential tariff would not be justified under the text of the said convention.
So there is a clear understanding as to that.
