Commercial Treaties

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 203, respecting trade between Canada and Esthonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Portugal, Rou-mania, and the Serb, Croat and Slovene Kingdom.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will make an explanation with reference to this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is similar to the bill dealt with yesterday, with some exceptions. The United Kingdom has made various commercial treaties with world powers, most of them being styled " for commerce and navigation," and it is a general term of these treaties that they do not apply to the self-governing dominions unless the dominion gives notice that it intends to accept the treaty in whole or in part. In treaties with the foregoing countries it has been deemed advisable to accept the clause providing for the mutual exchange of the mostfavoured-nation treatment.
Let me give the committee the figures of our trade with these countries for the fiscal years 1926 and 1927. In 1926 our exports totalled $1,250,693, as against imports of $433,350; and in 1927 the relative figures were $2,374,021 as against $673,760.
In the classes of goods that we export our chief competitor is the United States, which enjoys the most-favoured-nation treatment with each country. [DOT] As our exports are considerably in excess of our imports from these countries, the benefits, both present and potential, are obvious. Several of the countries in question are new, and from time to time there is a gradual adjustment of tariff barriers, and as the United States is entitled to the most-favoured-nation treatment that country would immediately get the benefit of any local adjustment. Canada is now being placed on an equal footing with the United States.
This is the tariff position in each of the countries affected:
Esthonia has recently adopted minimum and maximum tariff schedules. The minimum rate is 50 per cent less than the general.
Hungary. Hungary has one tariff but has special treaty rates with a number of countries. There is also a provision that she can increase the normal rates three times where there is tariff discrimination against her goods.
Latvia. Latvia has now introduced a two-column tariff, the preferential being 50 per cent less than the general.
Portugal. Portugal has two rates, the maximum being generally double the minimum, although sometimes it is greater.
Roumania. Roumania has two rates, and it is provided that non-treaty countries may be called upon to pay the maximum, which is 50 per cent higher than the minimum.
The Serb, Croat and Slovene Kingdom. This kingdom has two rates. The maximum if often three times the minimum.
Lithuania. Early in 1926 Lithuania amended its customs tariff so that goods coming from non-treaty countries might be made subject to a duty of 30 per cent over the present one-column schedule. This new rating was never put into effect, but now that Latvia and Esthonia have adopted conventional rates Lithuania may do the same.
On section one-Short title.

Mr. Chairman, I am at
a loss to understand how these particular treaties are going to benefit Canada. Great Britain is a free-trade country, and to-day a million and a quarter men are out of work there because of such treaties as these. In a fiscal sense we are in an altogether different position as compared with the mother country. This simply means that we are following in the footsteps of Great Britain and adopting free trade piecemeal. We have given away the Canadian home market to foreign producers, with the result that 700.000 Canadians have had to go to the United States to look for work. As representing an industrial constituency I protest vigorously against this way of doing business. We are simply opening our doors to all the countries under the sun and making Canada the dumping ground for their surplus products and manufactures under a favoured nation free trade policy. One cannot go into any department store in the city I come from without finding on the counters every variety of goods imported from all these countries as well as from the United States, produced under such conditions as it is impossible for our manufacturers to compete against. In these European and Asiatic countries there is depreciated currency and cheap labour and the conditions are such that the Canadian manufacturers are entirely at a disadvantage. Treaties like the Australian, the French and others which this government has entered into, can have only one effect, and that is to destroy our home market.
Commercial Treaties

There is nothing before us to show how this is going to affect the home market here or employment in this country. The result will be the abolition of such little protection as we have. If that is the object, why not strike protection off the books altogether? I attended a convention where the word "protection," I am sorry to say, was not mentioned in any resolution, and the particular resolution in which it should have appeared I opposed. This proposal before us at the present time simply means that we are going to open our doors to free trade with Europe, South America and other parts of the world. We are not given any information as to how agriculture and many of our basic industries will be affected. W'hat we have before us to-day is nothing else than a second budget; that is what it is. It seems that this year we are geting our budget piecemeal-a part prepared by Mr. Moore, a part prepared by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), and a part presented to us in these various favoured nation treaties. This parliament is in the economic position of adopting a "shut your eyes, close your mouth and see what I will put in it" free trade policy.
Why, I venture to say that half the members of this house do not know what they are voting for. Those hon. gentlemen who represent protectionist constituencies are not in the house to protect the interests of their electorate. It seems to me that the Liberal party is aiming at complete free trade such as exists in England. That is their platform -free trade, as they have it in England. As a matter of fact, they have all sorts of platforms, but their fiscal policy is a platform to get in on and not to stand on. As a consistent protectionist I absolutely protest against this sort of thing. I protest against favoured-nation treaties which are going to open the doors of this country wide to all the nations of the seven seas. On the pretext of something called " most favoured-nation treatment", we are making Canada the dumping ground for the surplus products of the rest of the world. The only country under the sun not favoured by this government is the Dominion of Canada; Canadians are the only people on the face of the earth who are not to enjoy any economic favours or a place in the sun. The result, as I say, is that 700,000 of our men are obliged to seek employment in the United States owing to economic reasons.
Linder the free trade favoured-nation policy pursued in Great Britain one and a quarter millions are receiving the dole and a million are out of work. But to-day England is beginning to find out her mistake; she is being

shut out of the markets of the world and is veering around to protection and the Safeguarding of Industries Act. England has lost the ship-building orders to the Germans, and many of her other basic industries are threatened. They will not be able to weather the storm. I was alone in protesting against such a policy when I attended the convention at Winnipeg and I am consistent to-day in again opposing a proposal which makes for free trade and adopts free trade as they have it in England, piecemeal, as an economic policy for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All we are doing is giving to the countries concerned the advantage of our most favoured-nation column. But perhaps the best answer I can give my hon. friend is to inform him that of all those in Canada who have urged the government to negotiate these treaties the strongest representations have come from large industries in the city represented by him. I have in mind two particular industries there, doing a considerable business, and I may quote without giving names-although there is no reason whj' the names should not be given-
Let us have the names.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, one is the rubber industry of Toronto, a very large industry in which my hon. friend is no doubt interested. I will quote an extract from a letter received from Mr. Thomas Bradshaw of the Massey Harris Company:
We are extremely anxious that we should extend our European business in every way possible, and especially to do so at the present time in tho&e countries which are beginning to import our goods. The situation we find is that in certain European countries where the United States has a more favourable agreement than Canada, goods are being imported from the United States such as we manufacture in Canada. Trade connections are being made and we are absolutely unable to sell and make favourable connections. We know that we are losing a number of good opportunities now, and we fear it will be very difficult indeed for us to make good these losses in future years because many of the valuable connections which might be concluded will be taken up by United States manufacturers.
That is an extract from a letter dated February 8, 1926, signed Thomas Bradshaw.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What about 1928? What is his view now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We cannot make a treaty in half an hour, you know. We have been negotiating all the time and this is the conclusion of our work.

Did these people ask you to extend all the privileges of the French treaty to these different nations in order to

Commercial Treaties
trade with them? That is what you are doing in this case, just as you did yesterday in the other case. That is exactly what you are doing. You are giving to these different small nations all the advantages of the French treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Admitting all that, we are getting something in return.
What are you getting?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You cannot sell unless you buy, and we are now selling to these countries, notwithstanding that we have no trade agreement with them. We are selling more than we are buying.
Keep on selling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But we wish to increase our trade. Now, I have given the spread in the different customs tariffs. It would take some time to run over the different countries to show the benefits to be derived.
The minister a moment ago spoke about the United States as our competitor. Is the United States giving to these people in its market the same advantages as we are extending to them in ours?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not what the United States are doing; it is what they are buying from us. That is what interests our industries; it is the fact that they can get in there on the same terms as other countries. And everyone knows that the more they can sell there, the better for them. Take the agricultural implement industry, for example. If that industry can run night and day, one part of the time on export business and the other part on domestic business, does it not stand to reason that it can sell cheaper in its own country? My hon. friend will agree with that.

I do not agree with that at all. I do not agree that any business can run profitably night, and day, except a few industries, such as steel. It is ridiculous to talk about businesses running night and day because it is not profitable to do so.

There are some people
who call themselves manufacturers, but who are really the worst enemies of the manufacturers in this country; they want to grab all the privileges, and they do not care what becomes of those people who are out of employment. No wonder the minister has read letters from them; they want to secure all the advantages there are from such a treaty at the expense of everyone else. We have
had unfortunate experiencs with regard to the last three or four treaties, and I predict that this will not be different.

The other side of the question should be explained by the minister, namely what imports we are likely to receive from these countries and how these imports will affect our own markets. The hon. gentleman said he was selling something to these central European countries. So he is; he is selling the labour markets of Canada to the extent to which these countries are placed at an advantage in our markets over our own producers. We are also told that this will provide a greater market for the manufacturers of rubber and of agricultural machinery, but I would not give the Canadian market as represented by prospective imports from central Europe in order to assist those two large combinations known as the rubber combine and the agricultural combine. The great need of this country at present is not to advance the interests in foreign markets of the combines and trusts of Canada; outside of our agricultural and mining production our great need is to foster and encourage the small industries which formerly operated in Canada, giving employment to the people in our small towns and country villages. If we are to retain our population and give employment to those who may come to Canada from abroad we must encourage these smaller industries which formerly gave local1 employment to thousands of people and kept them at home. Therefore I believe that before we pass this bill we should know what imports we are likely to receive from abroad, what imports are given a particular advantage in our market. Otherwise it seems to me we are giving them our markets without a quid pro quo, and the only satisfactory thing about the treaty is the fact that it can be rendered ineffective by giving six months' notice.

It is not often I agree with the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church), but I endorse everything he said to-day, and I endorse also the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan). I am not going to repeat their statements, but notwithstanding the representations made by the two large firms in Toronto who favour this treaty I think it would be far better for us to consider the thousands of other industries in the city of Toronto rather than those two combines which are getting everything from this government. The importations from these foreign countries will create a great deal of unemployment in
Commercial Treaties

Canada, and in addition to that everyone knows that every treaty we have made since this government came into power has been detrimental to the country as a whole. Unemployment is increasing every day, and I say this is the biggest farce in the world. Let England make all the treaties she likes, but let us sit quietly and do all the business we can without allowing foreign countries to dump their cheap goods into our markets. I never heard so much rot before and honestly I do not know how the minister can defend such a treaty. We know that since 1922 this government have been ruining the industries of this country, and in the end it will drive them all out of the country. It makes a man sick when he is accustomed to do business on the level.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps that is why the stocks of all the different industries in Canada are so high.
That is no sign of prosperity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I listened to my hon. friend; surely he need not interrupt me.
I have heard that repeated too often.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps that is why stocks
have increased in value, and perhaps that is why they are paying the same dividends although the shares have been split up. Perhaps that is why the great industries of our country are employing almost twice as manj' men as they employed in 1922, and perhaps that is why our exports have increased so enormously during that period.
But the minister must know very well that there are far more closed factories in Toronto now than there were in 1922, and there is not half the employment to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that, and no one else knows it.
That applies even to the Massey Harris Company, which has been propped up by this government

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps that is why they are building more houses-
Half of them are empty, and the same applies to the stores.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
You cannot get away with that kind of stuff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, if we take the

agreements as they come, Eslhonia is first. The imports from that country were fibrilla, flax fibre and flax tow. Those came in free; no duty at all was collected on them. We sold to Esthonia wheat flour, rubber manufactures, internal combustion engines, harvesters and binders, mowing machines, ploughs and other farm implements together with parts for such implements. Then we come to Hungary; the concession we have with regard to that country is of considerable value to the fishing industry and the manufacturing industry of Canada. The imports from that country were largely beans.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And we do not produce any beans in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We do, but we had a bean crop failure last year. When we have plenty of beans we can take care of our own requirements, but when we do not grow them here we have to buy them from some other country.

Was that the only article
imported?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Practically. The total value
of the imports for the year ending March 31, 1927, was $60,956, of which $58,000 represented beans. Then we come to Latvia; the imports from that country in 1923 amounted to $8,810, of which 87,286 entered under the free tariff. There tvere no imports in 1924, but in 1925 they amounted to $2,927, of which $2,844 came in free. I suppose that represented raw material for some of our industries. The total imports in 1926 amounted to $400 and they all came in under the free tariff column. In that same year we exported to Latvia articles to the amount of $528,765. From Lithuania in 1923 the total imports were $5,873. These came in under the free tariff column. They were required I imagine for some of our industries.
Why do you select 1923?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Our record commenced in
that year. In 1924 the total imports were $525. That is to say $525 came in free.

The industries did not
require as much trade that year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will answer that argument
just in a moment. In 1926 the total imports were $300.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The industries were
worse off still.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In 1927 they were getting
better. The imports amounted to $4,107.

Commercial Treaties

They are getting worse
all the time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, better.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
From Roumania the imports
in 1927 were $35,666. There were $7,473 worth of nuts, $23,256 worth of beans, and $4,937 of other articles. We sell them canvas shoes, rubber tires, canned fish, agricultural implements, automobiles and other articles amounting in all to just about half a million. Before sitting down there is a matter I should like to put on record. I noticed in the press this morning some comment on the payments that have been made to Canada by different countries to which Canada loaned money during the reconstruction period, and there seems to be some misunderstanding as to Roumania. Under the agreement entered into in 1919, Canada loaned to Roumania $20,449,084- at 5-J per cent interest, and repayable in five years. My hon. friend did not object to trading with Roumania. That was during the time the friends of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) were in power.
Mr. ClIAPLIN:	I do not object to trading with them now, but I do object to the terms on which we are trading.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Ah, but the terms now are
better than the terms in my hon. friend's time.
Not at all. The minister knows very well that that money was loaned as a war measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes?

There was no trading
about it, it was a war measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are paying their own
way now.

We are very glad to hear
it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Up to the end of 1922 Roumania had paid no interest and no principal. Negotiations were undertaken by Hon. Mr. Larkin with representatives of Roumania with a view to placing this debt on a better basis. An agreement was made under which the arrears of interest plus interest thereon, amounting in all to $3,520,636, were capitalized with the original principal and new bonds for the sum of $23,969,720 were issued to Canada. These bonds bear interest at 4 per cent and mature April 1st, 1968. There is provision for a sinking fund which would retire the whole issue by the maturity date. The service of these bonds-interest and sinking fund-is secured by a special export tax on
grain, payable in sterling. To date, interest payments have been received by Canada regularly on the due date to the amount of $5,273,290 in all.

I was much impressed with the remarks of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). It is all right for us as Canadians to consider our own products and whether we can market them, but we must remember that other countries are acting similarly and are seeking markets for their products. One of these countries, Lithuania, is a much smaller country than Canada with a population of 4,800,000, about one-half of our own. The articles they are endeavouring to sell are corn, cattle, hams, poultry, eggs, butter, timber, flax, linseed, hides and wool. Now as a Canadian I contend that our markets for butter, eggs and wool have been sufficiently invaded by the treaties already entered into without opening the door to every other country in the world to make inroads in our market which should be preserved for our own products.

I simply wish to remark in reply to the Minister of Finance that the imparts which we now receive from these countries is no indication whatsoever of the imports which we are likely to receive under the more favourable tariff which is being granted to them. Take every one of these countries if you will. Look at the discussions at the last Economic conference at Geneva last year and you will find that every country is looking to the preservation of its own markets for its own local industries in order to keep its labouring people at home. These treaties are simply breaking down every safeguard we have in Canada, and placing other countries in a most advantageous position to compete locally in our markets with such manufactures as they are able to develop.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There are two or three points to which I should like to direct attention. First, these treaties are not set out in the statutes but such portions of them as the minister thinks desirable are referred to. I do not think it is sound legislation to proceed in that manner and not have before us the treaties upon which these concessions are based. Some of the treaties are very old, One is dated 1914, another is dated 1923, and a third bears as late a date as 1927. What we in effect are doing is giving adherence to treaties about which we know nothing. It is not sufficient to say that we are giving our support to the trade portion of these treaties. Let us look at the preamble, and the preamble is an important part in this regard:
Commercial Treaties

Whereas by treaties of commerce and navigation or by agreements made by exchanges of notes between the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and the countries and on the date set out in the schedule to this act, it is provided that the stipulations of the said treaties or agreements respectively shall not be applicable to any self-governing dominion unless notice is given of the desire of His Majesty that the said stipulations shall apply to such dominion but that nevertheless goods of such dominion shall enjoy in each of the said countries respectively the same treatment as would be enjoyed by similar goods if produced in the United Kingdom so long as goods produced or manufactured in the respective countries are accorded in such dominion favoured-nation treatment; and whereas it is desirable that Canada should have the benefit of that portion of each of the treaties or agreements which provides for the exchange of the said mutual trade advantages: Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
Now the effect of that is what? I ask the minister to state definitely what the effect of this notification or expression of desire to deal with these several countries is? Are we bound by all the provisions in the treaties or are we bound by portions of them only? If we are bound by portions of them only, how can that be having regard to the terms of the treaties themselves? The excerpts that are set out in the explanatory notes certainly throw no light upon that point There are references to particular articles of the treaty by which it is provided that the treaty itself shall not apply to self-governing communities nor to India, except under certain conditions. I should like to know whether or not we are bound by all the terms of the treaty merely because we give notice in that particular regard? It will be noticed that with respect to Esthonia, article 28 provides:
Nevertheless, goods produced or manufactured in India or in any of His Britannic Majesty's self-governing dominions, colonies, possessions or protectorates shall enjoy in Esthonia complete and unconditional most-favoured-nation treatment so long as goods produced or manufactured in Esthonia are accorded in India or such self-governing dominion, colony, possession or protectorate treatment as favourable as that accorded to goods produced or manufactured in any other foreign country.
Have we the right to limit our adoption, or as was said yesterday, our acceptance of that treaty with that particular foreign country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is clearly understoood.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The trouble is that we have not before us the treaties themselves. It is a wrong principle to ask parliament to exercise its legislative powers with respect to certain sections of a treaty without our having before us the whole of the treaty that has been negotiated between the two con-

tracting countries. That is the first point. Then the minister has made the point that the export trade of the country will be greatly developed by the adoption of these treaties. May I point out to the minister that the argument he made with respect to the agricultural implement business is answered in the United States Commercial Intelligence issued only a few weeks ago. They say that to-day they are displacing Canadian implements in Canada to an extent they never did before; that the business of the United States was greater in agricultural implements last year than it was ever before in their history, and that the business which they do in Canada is greater than they do in any other part of the world. What is the minister doing in this case? He is displacing Canadian manufactured goods in Canada by those of a foreign country and he is endeavouring. to open up a foreign market, a market that may be destroyed overnight. Let me ask the minister this further question: How long are these treaties for? It is not stated in this bill how long they are for, there is nothing to indicate how long they may last, because I find that each of them is on a different basis. There is at the end of the bili a provision with respect to the legislation coming into force and the suspension of inconsistent laws; but when is it to be ended? Are we bound by the terms of the commercial treaties that England negotiated with these countries for a term of fifteen or twenty years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They may be terminated on twelve months' notice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Where is that to be
found?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the explanatory notes.
The third section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have different terminations but they are all covered.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Section 3 reads:
The governor in council may make such orders and regulations as are deemed necessary to carry out the provisions and intent of this act, and may upon giving six months' notice to the government of any of the countries mentioned in the said schedule of his intention so to do, order and direct that the favoured nation treatment accorded to such country by this act shall cease and determine, whereupon it shall cease and determine accordingly.
The point I make is that it is not competent for the Dominion of Canada to pass that section if the treaty itself says that it shall be a treaty that requires two or three years' or twelve months' notice. Each treaty has its own particular provision.

Commercial Treaties
There is another point in that regard to which I wish to direct the attention of the minister. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) the other day read certain paragraphs from the findings of the Economic conference at Geneva. That Economic conference adopted as a principle the view that treaties of trade and commerce should be of long date and they gave the reasons why. Now we say that we are negotiating a treaty, because that is what this amounts to, with these various countries, Lithuania, Esthonia, Latvia, from which we buy beans and other goods of that sort amounting, according to the minister, to $4,000 in one year. I believe one year it got up as high as $5,000, and in another it dropped as low as $300. When our business in agricultural implements in Canada has been displaced by United States goods, as it was last year, according to their statement, as it never was before in our history; when we cannot sell at home but are trying to sell somewhere else, and when suddenly those foreign countries give us notice that they are through with us, what is going to happen to our business in this country? That is a question which the minister should be thinking about. He is telling us how he is expanding Canadian trade. I suggest to him that he should endeavour to expand it at home instead of leaving Canadian agricultural implements to find markets in other parts of the world while the Canadian demand is being supplied by long trainloads of United States machines, the manufacture of which provides employment for United States workers. These foreign countries in which the minister is endeavouring to find markets for our goods are building up their industries by highly protective tariffs; they are endeavouring to produce goods in their own countries, and when that trade is lost to us we shall turn in vain to our country for a market that has been displaced by goods manufactured by the people of the United States. I suggest that the time has come when the minister should direct his attention to the filling of Canadian requirements with Canadian-made goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend argue that we should impose an increased duty on agricultural implements? Let us understand each other on this.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is the old story-draw a herring across the trail if you can. I will answer the minister's question. Parliament took the duty off agricultural implements and the price became higher. The material, the steel, the iron and everything else imported that went into those goods we gave a drawback upon not only for foreign trade but for local trade as well. Notwithstanding that
fact, the United States industry has displaced our Canadian implements to an extent that never occurred before in our history. The United States Commercial Intelligence for February, 1928, states that the greatest market the people of the United States have to-day for their agricultural implements is the Dominion of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How does my hon. friend propose to stop that?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Apart altogether from the fact that it is the business of the minister and not mine to stop it, I will tell him how I would do so. I would stop it by changing seats with the Minister of Finance. That is a very simple way too. I can only say this that if the party which I have the honour for the moment to lead were in power, these things would not continue. Further, we have in our hands what instruments, what tools, to use the words of an Englishman, to accomplish that end? We have the tariff, the excise tax, drawbacks, freight rates; we have in our hands all these things as tools that will enable us tlo see to it that this thing ends without increasing the cost to the consumer by a single dollar. Why is it that the price of agricultural implements has gone up in the last five years? Why has the price not gone down, if the argument of my hon. friend is sound? Why is it that the figures cited by the hon. member for London (Mr. White), the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson) and the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Kaiser), have not been controverted? Because they cannot be controverted, because they are taken from trade journals, because they are statements of fact. The minister says: If you were in power, would you impose a duty? It might be that a duty would be necessary, but I would Utilize the machinery of government and the power of this parliament to an extent that would secure us against the invasion by the people of the United States of our market and not compel us to go abroad to seek markets for our products.
When the Minister of Finance read a letter from the head of a great manufacturing concern dated in 1926, all he had to do was to take the figures for that same concern for 1927 and bring them up to date and he would find that, instead of expanding their trade in in this country, they are yielding it to their United States competitors; that they have taken over the J. I. Case Company in the United States so that they may be able to get some benefit from that in addition to the factory which they have in France, and that they are depending more and more upon their export business and less and less upon the
Commercial Treaties

domestic consumption which is being taken away from them by somebody else, owing to the fact that conditions are as they are.
What will happen when these markets are lost to us? There is one market that we have control of, and that is our own. There are six markets that we have not control of, and those are mentioned in the schedule of this treaty. That is the point we desire to make, and that is the point which the minister should keep in his mind. While he can legislate for Canada he cannot legislate for Esthonia and Latvia, and when they give notice to terminate the treaty, when they no longer receive our goods under the mosWavoured-nation treatment, we shall seek in vain for a channel for our trade, after we have developed a channel across 3,000 miles of sea and a long distance by land, and at the same time have neglected the opportunity at home, and had our home market taken from us by somebody else. I have upstairs-and I can get it for the minister; I showed it to him during the recent debate-the statement made by the Americans that they had established in this country last year the greatest channel of trade for their implements that they had in the world, and now we are going to Esthonia and Latvia with foreign shipments, foreign currencies, and all that is therein involved, and neglecting the market at home.
The Minister of Finance asks, what would you do? Would you put on a higher duty? My answer is very simple. I would do whatever is necessary to enable us to manufacture at home the goods required by the Canadian people, and it is not necessary to increase the cost to do it either. You may appeal to your agrarian friends from Saskatchewan and ask them to cheer loudly when you speak of low duty. You may appeal to the hon. member for Weybum, with his repeal of the order in council dealing with the values to be placed on vegetables and eggs, or to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni who asks for a duty on eggs and makes his recital as a free trader that the duty would not increase the price. You may tell the cotton industry in Quebec that it is necessary to have a duty of 7^ per cent on yarns, and then abandon it because the agrarians demand that you should do so. You may do all that, but in the end this humbug will be understood by the people. This is nothing more or less than the old story; it has been practised so long in this country that it has become a habit with the minister. He appeals to the agrarians with one tale, and to the manufacturers with another, hoping to hold them both. If he wants to know what the market gardeners of Quebec think about it, let him ask that delegation

that is about to wait upon the Prime Minister headed by the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville; let him ask the agrarians from Saskatchewan whether they are going to let the order in council go or have it re-enacted; or ask my hon. friend from Laprairie-Napier-ville whether he is going to see the market gardening industry of Quebec destroyed. The humbug will end at last. To the left you have those who insisted on having the order in council rescinded. My hon. friend from Wey-burn has a smile on his face, like the cat that came in with the canary. He realizes that he has been successful in having the order in council cancelled. My hon. friend from Laprairie-Napierville is not smiling, because he has discovered what the cancellation of the order in council means. Yes, I see him smiling now, to think of the reception that his delegation will get from the Prime Minister and the cabinet when they ask for the re-enactment of the order in council and my hon. friend over there from Marquette is wondering what is going to happen; is the government going to rescind it and then re-enact it the same session? Is my hon. friend from Weyburn to have the pleasure of Seeing it rescinded in the early pant of the session, and then reintroduced and passed in the dosing days of the session? Is protection to be made effective on market gardening by order in council after the house prorogues? Ask the hon. gentleman who heads the delegation. Ask him what speech he will make when he presents the delegation to the Prime Minister and his colleagues.
It is the same old story, Mr. Speaker. Here we have it again in connection with these treaties of trade and navigation to carry Canadian goods into the far recesses of Austria, Esthonia and Latvia and the other communities that came into being by reason of the treaty of peace. But while all this is happening, what about Canadian markets? That is the problem we are putting to the hon. Minister of Finance, and it is a problem with respect to which we have a right to an answer. The hon. Minister of Justice, whom I see in his seat, smiling urbanely as ever, appealed the other day to Caesar, Caesar being the league of nations. May I ask him if he has read what the economic conference said about negotiating treaties of this kind with a short life? It was said that they should not be subject to easy termination because the channel of trade that may be destroyed makes great difficulties for both parties. After we have been sending our goods to Esthonia and Latvia, when that channel of trade is suddenly terminated by the people of those countries saying they do not need

Commercial Treaties
our goods any longer, the Canadian manufacturer will look in vain for his market at home, for he will have lost it to the United States of America. That is the position we put to the minister, and he rises in his wrath and asks, would you put a duty on agricultural implements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not wrathy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Then perhaps he is
righteously indignant. He asks, would we put a duty on agricultural implements. I answer, we would do anything that may be necessary.
Louder.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am so glad that my
hon. friends are interested in what I am saying. Per adventure it may be the rescinding of an order in council that I am speaking of.
I do suggest to the hon. Minister of Finance that we have a right to see what is involved with respect to the various terms for the termination of these agreements, for obviously we cannot by mere statute change the terms of the agreements. They date back to 1914, I believe. Lastly, it is quite apparent from what has been said that this is but a little more of what the great Napoleon described as ammunition, as fodder with which to feed the electorate as to the vast foreign trade developed by this country-830,000 worth of beans one year, and $500 worth of something else next year.
My hon. friend took occasion to refer to the loan to Roumania, and to the fact that in this morning's press adequate appreciation was not expressed of the great services of this government in collecting the interest from Roumania. Does he recall how we were condemned as a party because we loaned the money to Roumania? Does he recall the speeches, embalmed in Hansard, that were made against the Minister of Finance of that day and his supporters regarding the loan to Roumania? It was money lost and gone forever, he then said, and now he rejoices in the fact that, like the poor woman, Roumania has found her treasure again. He says it is due to the genius of the Liberal government because they reduced the interest from 5 to 4 per cent, and the Hon. P. C. Larkin was the genius who has discovered that Roumania can pay her interest. Does the Minister of Finance recall his speeches of those days condemning the loan to Roumania? I should judge from the smile of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he did not think much of the loan to Roumania.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not think much of it yet.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No, but unfortunately
the Minister of Finance was rejoicing in the fact that his High Commissioner in London has been able to negotiate an arrangement by which the loan is perfectly safe beyond peradventure.'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. I said that we had
collected 85,000,000 outstanding, and when we came into office not one cent of interest or principal had been collected.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Of course not, for the
loan had been made only a short time before. The loan was made to Roumania during her reconstruction period on the understanding that credits were to be available in Canada to give employment to Canadian workingmen during the period of reconstruction in this country. That credit having thus been used, there was some difficulty in the days of reconstruction for Roumania, but very shortly afterwards she found her feet and now every day is making progress towards stability. The Hon. Mr. Larkin told me in London what had been negotiated a few days before with Roumania, and that there had been assigned to this particular debt the proceeds of an export tax upon wheat. Now, wheat is one of the most important exports of Roumania, and we have this export duty upon wheat for the service of this loan. Our interest is being paid promptly, a sinking fund is provided, and the loan is safe. Yet my friend the Minister of Finance takes responsibility for having reduced the interest rate to four per cent and accepted new securities for the old. I am sorry my friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce has so little confidence in the loan with regard to which there has been a complete novation; the loan now is the loan of this government and not of its predecessors. But I think the hon. gentleman should at least say that those who made the loan had high faith and confidence that it would ultimately be repaid, and that it was made by us as an international obligation and duty and to give employment at that particular period of reconstruction to a large number of Canadian workmen. The government of that day believed the loan was well secured. It now transpires that it was safe in every particular, and although the government have reduced the rate of interest to four per cent, they probably did so for reasons perfectly good to themselves, because they compounded some of the old interest. I wish my hon. friend a long life of peace and happiness in some other office than that which he now occupies, for in that event he will be with us until 1968 when the securities mature.

Commercial Treaties

The Minister of Finance
a few minutes ago, replying to an hon. member on this side of the house, stated that there was very little unemployment in this country. Again and again the members of this party are accused of being unpatriotic because we have drawn attention to the obvious fact that there is unemployment in the Dominion. I have in my hand the Canadian Unionist, the organ of the All-Canadian Congress of Labour, and I propose to quote its opinion on the question of employment in this country which the minister says is in such excellent condition. The article begins:
The government spokesman, moving the adoption of the address in the House of Commons on January 27, declared that "unemployment was considerably lessened and the demand for labour has increased."
Then a little lower down I find the following:
The desire to minimize the prevalence of unemployment is shared by both the old-line political parties.
I read that passage to show that this paper is not the mouthpiece of the Conservative party; it is a labour organ pure and simple.
Again:
Nowhere can one obtain statistics of unemployment that have any claim to accuracy or completeness, without collating the reports of at least two government departments.
And again:
The prosperous condition of Canadian industry is proclaimed from high places: the partial returns on unemployment are quoted as though they revealed the whole situation. But casual observation is sufficient to convince one that prosperity is confined to comparatively few among the population and that unemployment is rampant among the masses.
In another part of the article the writer estimates that the unemployed in the cities and towns of Canada amount to a quarter of a million. He says:
To sum up the situation of the Canadian working class:	the dry-as-dust figures from
official sources speak with a horrible eloquence, and they prove beyond dispute that among more than one-third of the workers (the only section for which statistics are available) unemployment is rife. Applied to the remainder of the workers by simple rule-of-three, they show that a quarter of a million urban wage earners are involuntarily idle and suffering from unmerited poverty.
And he concludes:
-and government spokesmen. . . are contemptible indeed when they seek to beguile the public with platitudes about a "prosperity" that is a delusion and a snare.
I have quoted the article, Mr. Chairman, because continually we on this side of the
t.Mr. Bennett.]
house are accused of exaggerating any ill conditions in the Dominion and are taunted with being unpatriotic in drawing attention to undoubted facts. Only a few minutes ago the Minister of Finance made the broad statement that Canadian employment is good and that no one could deny it. Well, the Canadian Unionist denies it. It reminds me of other broad statements the hon. gentleman has made without adducing the slightest proof of their soundness. Again and again he has told this house that his tariff reductions last year did not do any harm to the motor industry of Canada. Yet the Department of Trade and Commerce has issued statistics that the manufacture and export of automobiles has decreased and the import of automobiles has increased. Those figures I placed on Hansard some time ago. I bring this to the attention of hon. members because I believe general statements of this character made by the minister should be backed up with ample proof, and that the government should hesitate to accuse the official opposition of. unpatriotic motives simply because we have described conditions as they actually exist, and as confirmed by this labour organ.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Before this bill passes I
should like to discuss the merits of it. Last session a bill similar to this was introduced into the house, its purpose being to increase the capital stock from $2,000,000 to $4,000,-
000.	We who opposed the bill at that time both in the banking and commerce committee and on the floor of the house maintained that the real purpose of the bill was to increase the profits of the shareholders at the expense of the participating policyholders. This contention was upheld by the Superintendent of Insurance, and with due respect to that gentleman I think he is generally recognized as one of the outstanding financial men in the Dominion of Canada. He is a man who cannot be swayed by anything other than his own good judgment. We often hear references made in vague and indefinite terms to the influence of the big interests on the governing body in this Dominion, and I was glad indeed that parliament saw fit to block that proposed legislation, which was obviously unfair not only to the policyholders of the company, but to the insurance business in general.
The contention that the main purpose of the bill was to increase the profits of the stockholders was denied by the sponsors of the bill, who waxed wrathy at the mere suggestion of any such thing, but those who were in favour of the bill were put to the test by an amendment moved by a member of the Progressive group proposing a 15 per cent profit limitation on the proposed new capital. The amendment was endorsed by the Minister of Finance, who said at the time that after all it was the policyholders' money which provides the real capital of the company. He

Sun Life Company
also said that a 15 per cent profit limitation was not an unfair rate of interest on any legitimate investment. The amendment was carried, and immediately the bill was withdrawn. Anyone who had had any question in his mind up to that point as to the real purpose of the bill certainly was in doubt no longer. The fact that the company withdrew its bill and refused to accept the 15 per cent limitation was a complete admission on the part even of the company itself that the real purpose of the bill was to re-arrange the company's stock so as to exact a greater profit, and to do that with the authority of parliament. The company is back this year with a bill of a similar nature, but this time they have carefully paved the way. A reorganization of the directorate has taken place and men of political prominence now sit on the board, it being expected, no doubt, that they will in some way or other be able to facilitate the passage of this bill through the house. On top of that, the best lobbyists were obtained, and they canvassed members before the bill was even introduced. I believe that this has been the most thoroughly lobbied bill in the House of Commons that I have seen so far. If one were to judge by the enthusiastic support this bill received in the banking and commerce committee, those who are opposed to it must be a small minority, but we are not discouraged, and we hope to stir up enough opposition so that the policyholders will take some action and their sentiments perhaps be reflected in some way or another on the floor of this house. We are encouraged by the fact that the Superintendent of Insurance is again opposed to this bill, in face of the fact that a press report, emanating no doubt from the head office of the Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada, appeared some time ago to the effect that some agreement had been reached with parliament by which the passage of this bill was assured. This report, I believe, was responsible for the stock of the company, which stood at that time at $560 per share, soaring to its present value of $2,000 per share. Before passing this bill in its present form parliament must consider this matter very carefully because certain principles are at stake.
Canada stands second among the nations of the world to-day in per capita life insurance. Life insurance is a real economic necessity. It is of national importance, and is rendering a service comparable only to that rendered by our chartered banks and trust companies, and from a humanitarian standpoint it gives protection to widows, children and dependents. The operation of life insurance companies should therefore be supervised
and guarded closely. This company is attempting a stock manipulating scheme which is not in the best interest of the policy-holders or the insurance business generally. To-day, when the whole trend of events in the insurance world is towards mutualization, the Sun Life company is asking permission of this parliament to increase its capital. Those who have taken out insurance with the company have done so on the present basis of operation. If we pass this bill, we will be a party to a breach of contract between the company and the policyholders. It is useless to argue that this increase in capital will not be a tax upon the policyholders. To bear out this contention I would refer to the evidence of Mr. Macauley, given before the royal commission on insurance. Under oath before this commission he stated, in reply to a direct question, that he had been repeatedly requested to allow shareholders to pay up more money and had refused, (1) because the company did not need the money or capital; (2) because the new capital would be taking away more of the profits belonging to the policy^ holders.
To use his exact words, he stated:
The reason that guided me particularly in refusing was always that it would be a tax on the policyholders.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: May I ask if the hon. gentleman is a policyholder in the Sun Life company?

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, I am. In 1901 the Canada Life Assurance Company increased its paid up capital from $125,000 to $1,000,000. The president of the Sun Life company at the time issued a circular in which in caustic and severe terms he criticized the action of the Canada Life company in that regard. Referring to the part which dealt with the direct effect of an increase of capital of $875,000 upon the Canada Life policyholders, he stated:
And now let us see the extra amount of profits that the change will cause to be absorbed. On an 8 per cent basis, half of the interest on the paid up capital $40,000, will likely be taken from the policyholders' earnings, which is $35,000 more than in the past. Therefore the policyholders will be mulcted yearly to that extent. On a 20 per cent basis the policyholders' annual loss would reach $175,000.
How does that harmonize with the president's statement that the policyholders cannot suffer in any way whatever by the calling in of the capital stock.
That was what the president of the Sun Life thought of the action of the Canada Life at that time. What must the company honestly think of itself to-day, when it has not only called in its unpaid capital, but is actually asking parliament to let it issue more
Sun Lije Company

capital stock? The calling in of the unpaid capital stock, and the issuing of new stock, brings up another matter upon which some light should be thrown.
At the time the Canada Life Assurance company increased its paid capital its shares were quoted at $525. The minute the $875,000 was paid in, according to the president of the Sun Life, the market value of the stock became $4,593,000, and to use his own words:
The shareholders would seem to pocket the whole benefit of the difference of $3,718,000, and seemingly all for the best interest of the policyholders, another admirable illustration of the administration of a great trust maintaining the people's interest even against their opinions.
Now I agree that the president of the Sun Life was perfectly right at the time. It was a get-rich-quick scheme. To-day Canada Life stock stands around $1,200 per share, and those same stockholders have been enriched by a further four million dollars or so.
But the point I want to make is this. If the president of the Sun Life was right at the time, and he surely was, how does it apply to-day to his own company? A few months ago the Sun Life increased its paid up stock to its full authorized capital, from $1,500,000 to $2,000,000. Its stock is quoted at approximately $2,000 per share. On a 20 to 1 basis its $500,000 paid in is now worth ten millions. Therefore the shareholders in question benefited by the transaction to the extent of $9,500,000 on the present market values, the interest on which is borne by the policyholders. If the two millions of new capital stock asked for in this bill is issued at par, with a fixed dividend of 25 per cent, and enjoying a share of the reserve fund now the property of the shareholders, it will mean that the marketable value will be at many millions, which will mean another melon the interest upon which will be borne by the policyholders.
Mr. Macauley, the present president of the company, is an astute business man, and in order to facilitate the passing of the bill has conceived the brilliant plan of throwing up a smoke screen, and so he says that the Americans are trying to buy up control of the company. The patriotic appeal is the last resort. Since 1911, however, the old flag-waving stuff has lost its punch. The Superintendent of Insurance points out that if the Americans were trying to buy up the stock, which is not the case, the two millions of new capital asked for is not necessary to protect the company from such a contingency.
It might be interesting to point out the inconsistency of the Sun Life in this respect- about as inconsistent as many of the arguments advanced by some of our opposition

friends in regard to trade treaties.	They
appear to entertain the idea that they can make a hole in the fence big enough to let their chickens through into their neighbour's garden, but not big enough to let their neighbour's chickens trespass in their own gardens. From information under my hand 1 find that the Sun Life has money invested in 233 foreign concerns, mostly American, and on top of that a fair share of their insurance business is done in the United States. The company has twenty thousand shares of fully paid up stock, and at the present time sixty-five people own 15,126 of these shares, or over 75 per cent; and 194 people own the balance of 4,874 shares, or about 25 per cent of the capital stock. So with the whole of the capital stock in the hands of so few people, it is quite obvious to me that there is no danger of any outsiders obtaining control against the wishes of the present shareholders. Their whole argument in this regard lacks force and reason, and may well be treated lightly.
A brief statement of the company's affairs shows that the original paid up cash capital was $305,000. From that small sum of money the company's business was built up. Special dividends and stock bonuses have been declared, bringing the capital stock prior to January of this year up to $1,500,000. To do this they divided a stock bonus of $845,000 and declared a special dividend of $350,000. On the actual capital of $305,000 they have been declaring dividends annually of $225,000, or at the rate of 73.8 per cent on the actual cash investment. At the same time the company has been piling up a huge reserve, which is the property of the shareholders. On January 1 of this year the marketable value of the 15,000 paid up shares was $30,000,000. So the cash investment of $305,000 has grown in value by nearly a thousand times the original amount. Now, I think that is nearly enough for the company to have, and that a halt should be called in their manipulations. Stock manipulations and stock watering are all too common in this country, the result being that the Canadian public is weighted down to-day paying interest on tremendous capitalizations of this kind, built up by manipulations and profits taken from the people themselves.
Referring again to the financial record of the company, a few years ago when it was necessary to increase the capital in order to operate in the American market they issued their new stock at a premium, and properly so, of $300 per share. This premium went where it should go

to the policyholders. There is no intention on the part of the company this time to divide the money with the policyholders,

Sun. Life Company
to whom it rightly belongs. On the contrary, according to the bill this stock will be issued at par to their friends, and immediately it assumes a market value they will make a profit ranging from ten to forty million dollars by the transaction.
I understand that the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) proposes to move an amendment that the capital stock to be issued be held in trust for the policyholders.
I am quite prepared to support this amendment, but on general principles I would rather see the bill thrown out entirely. Therefore I reserve my right to vote for the amendment, but if there is sufficient support I shall vote for the rejection of the bill itself.

maintopic: SUN LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I also
wish to add my voice in protest against the passage of this bill. The hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Hepburn) has gone into the activities of the company so thoroughly that I need not quote any figures. I will content myself with the broad statement that in my opinion this is an effort to water the. stock in order to make some money for the company without its rendering any service whatever in return. Further, I hold that it is the duty of the government to regulate such activities. The government is entrusted with the welfare of the people of Canada, and in view of the fact that under the law it is an offence not to have any money at all, I argue that correspondingly it should be an offence to have too much money. If a Canadian strolls into any city or town of this Dominion and is found to be without this "visible means of support" he will be arrested. Now, it seems to me that it is reasonable to argue conversely that if anyone in this country has too much money, and has not obtained it honourably, he also should be subject to the same treatment as the beggar. Only parliament can determine the ways by which it may be permissible for any citizen of Canada to obtain money. Therefore I think an application of this kind should be scrutinized very carefully to make sure that it is not an attempt to get the privilege of passing out to the shareholders a huge amount of money without rendering any corresponding service therefor.
It is worth while, Mr. Chairman, to consider the reasons advanced by the company for this increase in their capital stock. I well remember that a short time ago it was argued in the press that in order to enable this company to go into foreign fields and underwrite insurance and engage in other business activities it was necessary to increase the capital stock. Well, at the present time
Canada is making very strenuous efforts to induce foreign capital to be invested in the development of this country. So long as we are going to the four comers of the earth to induce capitalists to invest their money in Canadian enterprises, why should we make it easy for the Sun Life Company to invest their funds in foreign countries? Then the previous speaker touched on another matter. He stated that the newspapers a little while ago carried a notice from the president of the company that there was grave danger of the Americans getting control of the company. I remember having read some of these articles. The president would evidently lead the Canadian people to believe that in some secret, unseen manner the Americans were going to come over and simply steal this Canadian company. Anyone who has gone into the history of the company to any extent will realize that the directors had it in their own power to keep the Americans or anybody else from doing anything of the kind. Until a short time ago only 75 per cent of the stock had been fully paid up. The directors had control of the transfer of shares until such time as the shares were fully paid up. If they wanted to maintain this as a Canadian company and to retain practically the same shareholders as were formerly in the concern, all they had to do was to refrain fiom calling for the last 25 per cent on the shares. But a few months ago they sent out a call, and the remaining 25 per cent was paid up. Now the directors have no say in the matter and the shares may be transferred without their approval, so that there is an opportunity now for the shares to get into the hands of others than Canadians. That there is a possibility of this happening is a different matter.
It is worth while considering the very great advance that has taken place in the shares of the company. A few months ago the shares were somewhere around $600 or $700; at the present time they are about $2,000. Do hon. members think that the investing public of this country and of the United States sat down and figured out the possible earnings of the company within the next few months and, after looking into the matter more thoroughly, decided that, whereas, a few months ago the company had an earning power which would justify the payment of $600, now it has an earning power on its shares that will yield a value of $2,000? Will anyone argue for a moment that there is any possibility in the world that the investing public of this country came to the conclusion, after mature deliberation, that Lhese shares were worth that much more than they were a few months previously?
Sun Life Company

One thing more I wish to touch upon. This possibly has been one of the most successful companies we have ever had in Canada. It operated for a considerable time on a very small capital; in fact, until 1897 it had a paid-up capital of only $30,000. Now if they have been getting along so marvellously well on so small a capitalization, is it not rather risky to give them the privilege of materially increasing their capitalization, especially at a time such as we are passing through, particularly having regard to the investments that are offering? All companies are liable to make indiscreet investments, and while this is an ably managed company and all that, parliament owes a duty to the shareholders and policyholders of the company and would do well, I submit, to discourage this endeavour. We owe this to the policyholders at least, in order to ensure that they snail receive that consideration to which they are entitled.
Possibly no other company in Canada has made money more quickly or has gone further afield to make it. We find that the Sun Life has investments practically throughout Europe and North America. If increasing the capital stock is going to facilitate these foreign investments, I Should think it would be very much better if we left the stock where it stands. Possibly no country in the world today requires capital more than Canada does, and certainly none is making a greater bid for it. It is almost nine o'clock, Mr. Chairman. I submit that this question should be given very serious consideration. It would be a grave mistake for this house to pass a measure like this without considering it thoroughly, and in view of the fact that we have had only half an hour to-night to discuss the subject, I move that the debate be adjourned.

I shall take only a few
minutes of the time of the committee on this bill. The principle of the bill is laid down in its preamble. This company is in a good financial condition. Mr. Kellner.]

Before the house rose at six o'clock I asked the minister to give some of the information which he must have collected during the negotiation of these treaties, and his answer was that we were supposed to know that the products of these different countries were mainly agricultural. I suppose the minister was referring to beans, which seem to have been the product most in evidence as coming from any one of these countries Other articles cited by the minister came in free. But that gives us no information at all as to the possible effect on the trade of this country of the agreements now contemplated. Probably the minister had something to do with the negotiation of these treaties, and I think he owes it to the house to give some of the information he thus acquired. It is no help to us to give the exports from these different countries to Canada under the old tariff; we want to know the probable or possible effect of the new tariff upon the agricultural and industrial life of this country, and we can secure that information only by learning what are the products of these countries and to what extent and under what conditions they have been exported to other'countries, such as Great Britain. I do not know where the agreements were negotiated; we have had no information in that regard. Probably they were put through by half a dozen trade commissioners and concluded by correspondence between the different capitals. These agreements may have a disrupting effect on the industries of this country; we do not know. If the minister has been closely in touch with the negotiations no doubt he has weighed the possible advantages and disadvantages which may result in the future, so I would like him to answer that question a little more fully. It is not well to pass it off by saying that we are supposed to know that the products of those countries are mainly agricultural. If the minister knows that they are or are not such, let him say so, but we are entitled to have some statement from him as to the probable effect upon the commerce of the country.

Prime Minister asked me what we have been exporting. Ah, Mr. Chairman,, no question could better prove my case, for it proves that while the American manufacturer has been taking advantage of the market near at home, the Canadian manufacturer has been forced to ship his product three thousand miles by sea and thousands of miles by land to find a market to replace his home market captured by his competitor to the south as I have read from the United States report. the language used by the right hon. Prime Minister just one year before he was forced- forced, I	say-by his supporters from

What is the position with regard to the United States? Is there any member of this house who will stand up in his place and say: Notwithstanding that obvious fact we think we should throw down our bars against the United States and give them an opportunity to come in here and affect our industries in a manner even more seriously than they have already been affected.
That was the question! propounded by the Prime Minister in 1923. In 1924, yielding to pressure to put these items on the free list, he appeased the manufacturers when they complained by giving them free raw material, free ore, free steel. The result has been that we have decreased the quantity of agricultural implements produced in Canada by upwards of 10 per cent since this tariff came into force. In other words, we have bought from foreign lands 10 per cent more of our agricultural implements than we were purchasing at the time this legislation was enacted, with no advantage to the farmer inasmuch as prices have not been lowered. The facts placed on Hansard by the hon. member for London (Mr. White) the other night cannot be controverted; they cannot possibly be denied. The trade journals which the hon. member produced, giving references to page and date, abundantly establish his contention. There is no dioubt about this; the figures conclusively prove it. It may foe said, as has been said frequently in the past: "Oh, well, we are a low tariff party; we are reducing the tariff on implements of production",-then turning to the manufacturer and saying: "We will not hurt you; we will give you a drawback on everything you import, so that while it may appear that we are reducing the tariff we are in reality affording you greater protection than ever".

It is the same in regard to fertilizers and other things as well.
