That is my opinion in that regard and there is no need for apology.
The Minister of Finance in the treaty he has introduced to-day has been careful to avoid dealing with the subject directed to his attention by the hon. member for Cariboo. He realizes that in respect of many of the articles to which reference has been made he

Commercial Treaties

is bringing about, in this instance, the same condition that resulted in relation to the Australian treaty with respect to raisins and other commodities. In other words, by giving a blanket concession, absolutely regardless of the details of his agreement, he is incurring the risk of having our markets destroyed with respect to such commodities as may be produced in the countries with which he is dealing. Now we are endeavouring to develop our resources. As the Prime Minister asks, if the markets to the south of us are shut off by the Fordney-McCumber tariff or any other policy that may be adopted in the United States, what happens? Here we are adopting a blanket policy with respect to these various countries with which we are making agreements, and the only stipulation we make is that the lowest tariff we give to any people in the world, with the exception of the British tariff, shall be extended to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And they say they will give the same tc us.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, they say that they will give us the lowest tariff they have. But I submit that the treaty is in its essence wholly wrong because it pays no regard to the varying circumstances and conditions prevailing respectively in the two contracting countries. I do not think a treaty is sound which provides a blanket concession such as this. It was not customary in days gone by to negotiate treaties in this form; it was customary to name the articles affected and to determine the measure of duty that should be applied. What we have done is this: we have gone to these countries and said, "You give us your best tariff and we will give you that tariff which is most favourable to you." Bear in mind that the League of Nations, to which the Minister of Finance made reference this afternoon, has stated that the only country in the world that has reduced its tariff since the war is Canada. We have a lower tariff than any of these six nations affected. If we are the only country that has reduced its tariff since the war, and these new states that came into being by reason of the doctrine of self-determination have erected, according to the report of the economic conference, high tariff walls for the purpose of endeavouring to render their communities self-sustaining and self-contained, it is obvious at what a disadvantage we have placed ourselves. Willy-nilly we are making a blanket arrangement by which we say to them, "You give us the lowest you have and we will give you the lowest we have." But as Senator Dandurand says, Canada has reduced its tariff three times since the war, and

- it follows therefore that our tariff is relatively low to those of the various countries involved. My hon. friend from South Toronto, who is desirous of ascertaining the tariff rate with respect to some of these items, has asked for certain figures. We had certain figures given to us yesterday, but none have been volunteered to-day. We do not know what the tariff is in relation to Esthonia or Latvia or Lithuania or the country of the Serbs. We do not know what their tariff is on the various items involved; we have no idea what intermediate tariff they levy. In negotiating this treaty, to which we are asked to give our approval, the minister has offered us nothing in any shape or form to indicate what duties are imposed by these foreign countries. We know of course that they have varying tariffs; they have high tariffs and low tariffs; some have intermediate tariffs and others have not. Others again have one tariff against the world. But we have undertaken to accept the lowest tariff from them, whatever it may be, and we are giving them in return-apart from the British preferential tariff-a rate lower than that we shall enjoy from any of them. Aud this we are doing regardless of any other consideration. I submit that is not a proper basis on which to negotiate a treaty. For instance, we should know exactly whether, by reason of such a treaty, raisins are to cost us $2 or $3 per pound in duties. Had we known that when the treaty was negotiated with Australia, the situation would have been different, because there are many admirable things in connection with that treaty. I suggest, however, rhat if the minister had had the knowledge of bargaining he should have had, he would not not have made that agreement with respect to raisins. He has said himself, and we have it on record, that when he went to Australia ne tried to raise the tariff so that he would have something with which to bargain, having in mind the very fact to which I now allude. So it is painfully apparent to us as the years go by that to place upon the statute book a treaty about which we have nothing before us to indicate the measure of the duties imposed is but to put our heads in a noose and leave the noose open. As a result some products may come in here more readily than they will go anywhere else, while at the same time we have the advantage of the lowekt tariff, whatever it may be ,in these countries in Europe. There is nothing to indicate that the protection is fair or just, and certainly it is a departure from the principles under which tariff treaties were negotiated in the early history of this country. For that reason

Commercial Treaties
we are directing attention to the undesirability of entering into blanket treaties with respect to trade which contain no specific reference to the various matters affected, and which do not allow this country to safeguard its industrial, agricultural and indeed its national life through this parliament. We have had occasion during the last few weeks and months to direct attention to the fact that the treaty negotiated with New Zealand by order in council has brought into Canada from the country during the last few months thousands of pounds of butter. I do not refer to the Australian treaty; I speak of a tariff treaty negotiated by order in council, with respect to which this parliament was not consulted. I submit that to negotiate commercial treaties in this way is to bring about injury to the economic life of this country which cannot be easily overtaken, because as he said not long ago my hon. friend realizes the difficulties with which he had to deal in considering the effect as regards raisins and the effect of the New Zealand treaty with respect to butter.
I do not want these cases to be similar in character, and for that reason we venture to point out the undesirability of negotiating blanket treaties with no reference to the articles affected, leaving the lowest tariff in each country to affect the imports into the respective countries without regard to the peculiar circumstances and conditions under which we maintain our national life.

speechtext: They would be interesting.

I make this suggestion,
although it will take a little mental arithmetic. We might take the exports and if we deduct from them-

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
All I want
is the bare increase in business.

I have not the figures
under my hand. I was endeavouring to suggest a way by which they might be arrived at. I am not saying that there has been no
fMr. C. A. Stewart.]
increase. I am saying that there has been a large increase in exports, but there has also been a tremendous increase in imports.
Let me deal now with imports of automobile parts. The figures are as follows:
Year	Imports
1923		 $14,000,000
1924		 16,000,000
1925		 14,000,000
That is an average of about $15,000,000 a year. Then in the second budget of 1925 we amended the tariff adjustments that were first introduced and we put certain parts and materials on the free list, with what result? The result was that importations of automobile parts increased in 1926 to $23,000,000 and, ini 1927, the figures for which the minister did not quote, to $29,000,000. What has been the .effect? The effect of the amendment to the tariff in 1925 has been simply to double our imports of parts entering into the manufacture of automobiles. Let me take some of the items. For instance, a line of manufacture .that is handled wholly in Canada is tops, wheels and bodies. I see no imports of these prior to 1925, but in 1926 we have an importation amounting to $6,000,000, showing a tremendous increase in this importation and naturally a loss to Canadian trade. The result ,of the whole thing is this, as my hon. friend .pointed out a moment ago: You closed up in Oshawa a malleable iron factory for a period of time. It is true they reopened that and are working again. In another section of Canada near Windsor there was a factory successfully manufacturing automobile tops, and this factory has been closed up and out of business ever since. Authorities that know tell me that in Ontario alone there are two hundred industries that are seriously affected by these amendments to the tariff. It is not sufficient to say that Massey-Harris, the International Harvester, possibly the General Motors and a few other large companies have compensated their loss in some other way, if other industries in other cities and towns have been seriously and adversely affected. That is our complaint. We say to the minister in regard to this treaty just as we said in regard to the treaty that was under discussion yesterday: We have no way of gauging its possible effect upon Canadian trade. Personally I am quite prepared to endorse the principle of making trade agreements with other countries; but I would want to use our bargaining power, that is our tariff, in making specific treaties with these different countries, getting some advantage in their market in return for an advantage ' offered in our market. But in this case we .are given nothing of the kind, and I venture to say that the minister has not an official

Commercial Treaties
in his department nor has the Department of National Revenue an official who can give us any idea of the possible effect of this treaty. This series of treaties will go into operation; imports will start to come in and then industries which are adversely affected will come pext year before parliament or before the government and plead for some redress in regard to the unfair competition to which they are subjected. That is not a reasonable way to legislate or to make treaties, and we are justified in complaining very bitterly that the minister is unable to give us any information regarding the possible or likely effect of this treaty. When the hon. member for South Toronto put his question to the minister this afternoon, it was a pertinent query that ought to have brought forth some response, I repeat what I said yesterday in regard to the treaty with Czechoslovakia, that we are blindly ratifying to-night these seven treaties without knowing any of their terms. Furthermore, we do not know to what we are committed in the way of navigation, because these are trade and navigation treaties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is nothing about navigation. We are accepting only the trade part.
Mr. STEVEN'S: It is very comforting to get that information from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would direct my hon. friend's attention to 'the preamble, which is very clear:
Whereas it is desirable that Canada should have the benefit of that portion of each of the treaties or agreements which provide for the exchange of the said mutual trade advantages.
That is all we accept.

I read this also in the preamble:
Whereas by treaties of commerce and navigation or by agreements made by exchanges of notes between the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and the countries and on the dates set out in the schedule to this act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the title.

No, it is the preamble.
It is provided that the stipulations of the said treaties or agreements respectively shall not be applicable to any self-governing dominion unless notice is given of the desire of His Majesty that the said stipulations shall apply to such dominion but that nevertheless goods of such dominion shall enjoy in each of the said countries respectively the same treatment as would be enjoyed by similar goods if produced in the United Kingdom so. long as goods produced or manufactured in the respective countries are accorded in such dominion favoured-nation treatment;

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Read on.

and whereas it is desirable that Canada should have the benefit of that portion of each of the treaties or agreements which provides for the exchange of the said mutual trade advantages: Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows: -
We have not a single article of the treaties before us except these articles which refer to the method by which we shall become a party to the treaty. That is the complaint we make, that the minister ought to have given the house copies of these treaties long ago so that we might have studied them carefully, together with information regarding trade other than just the bare imports and exports-because, after all, we are not making this agreement simply to deal with $300 worth of beans, which was mentioned in regard to one of the countries, but with the expectation of doing a growing business. If we expect to do additional business we want to know what direction that business is going to take. If we expect to increase our importations from these countries-and there can be no other object-we want to know what effect that is going to have on Canadian trade.
My hon. friend from Cariboo a moment ago drew attention to the question of beans. It raised a laugh in the house, but I want to say that I know that particular district and have known it for nearly thirty-five years. There are hundreds of farmers in that district, which is in what is known as the dry belt of British Columbia, who succeeded years ago in raising a very high quality of bean. It was their whole crop, and was just as important to them as the wheat crop is to the prairie farmer or the vegetable crop to farmers in other parts of the country. It was life or death to them, financially; it meant success or failure. Conditions were difficult for them because of competition from Japan and China, and the beans from those countries, by the way, were found upon examination in Canada to contain a certain poison, and there was a time when we had to shut those beans out of this country in the interest of the health of the people of Canada. There is now coming in from certain of the Balkan states what is known to be an inferior bean, a small yellow bean, which is not on a par at all with the beans we can produce in the district to which my hon. friend has referred and in other sections of Canada; they are not comparable at all, and yet our farmers are faced with this competition. The minister and others may say, what do the few beans we import amount to? But I say that it means all the difference between these farmers continuing in business or being driven out of business.

Commercial Treaties
It means spilling the beans.

Yes. It makes all the
difference in the world to them. It is a serious matter. I notice in the tariff which I have under my hand a long schedule of stuff coming in from Japan. Now the Japanese treaty of 1913, irrespective of what it contains, is to become our treaty with these seven different countries, and I ask the minister, does he know, in the light of the Japanese treaty, what the effect of these other treaties will be on Canadian trade. He may answer that he does not think they will have much effect. I do not know; I have not had time to check it up, but the point I am making is that both the French and the Japanese treaties become our treaties with seven other countries by one stroke of the pen, without the slightest information being furnished to parliament as to the possible effects. I submit that that is not fair to the people of Canada. Those in Canada who will be affected will not know it for one, two, three, four, six months, or perhaps a year, and then they will begin to realise that importers in Montreal and other parts of Canada are bringing in goods with which they cannot successfully compete. Someone may say, let us buy these goods in the cheapest market; but owing to the depreciated currency in these countries, and that factor, I am glad' to say, is lessening from year to year-
How does depreciated currency affect the situation?

The depreciated currency
of Europe has been one of the most serious factors affecting our trade. My hon. friend can shake bis head, but I know it; I have studied it from end to end. And not only is that a factor, but there are also the long hours of labour and the low wages paid in those countries. There is no gainsaying that their standard of living is lower than the Canadian standard. It is all very well to come forward . with this rather fantastic theory that the great desideratum should be to buy your goods in the cheapest market and sell them in the dearest, and then fold your arms and feel that you have propounded a profound philosophy, but as a matter of fact these things are not dealt with by theory; they are not determined by any philosophical reasoning, but by cold facts, competition and experience, and the experience of Canada will be suddenly to wake up and find that she has entangled herself in a dozen treaties in the last few hours which parliament is blindly ratifying without adequate information as to what the effects will be.
(Mr. Stevens.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend was for a short time-for altogether too short a time, I have no doubt he imagines-Minister of Trade and Commerce, and he knows the staff of the department fairly well. I think he will agree that among our best trade commissioners is Mr. Wilgress, who represents Canada as trade commissioner with headquarters at Hamburg. My hon. friend complains that we have no information before us from any of the officers of the department recommending treaties with these countries.

I did not say anything of the kind. I said that parliament has no information before it. The minister may have the information on his desk, but we have been discussing these matters now for two hours; one of these treaties we discussed for nearly two days, and I submit that, whatever information the minister has, it has not been placed before parliament.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have a letter from Mr. Wilgress dated September 21, 1926-possibly he was then writing to my hon. friend as minister-in which he says:
You will note that while Canadian goods are at present receiving the reductions, the Estho-nian government are awaiting official notification from Canada that most-favoured-nation treatment is being extended to goods of Es-thonian origin. I cannot too strongly urge that steps should be taken as soon as possible to officially notify the Esthonian government in the above sense, since there are practically no products which Esthonia could export to Canada, and hence the advantages would be all on the Canadian side if such a step was taken.
I admit at once that perhaps it might have been better had we had printed and distributed among the members more detailed information as to the difference in the tariffs, but as I pointed out on the introduction of the measure, we are obtaining concessions running from 10 to 50 per cent in the tariffs on our goods going into these countries. My hon. friend complains that this treaty is based on the treaty made with Japan, and he mentioned particularly beans. My hon. friend surely is not going to chide me over the Japanese treaty, which, was made by the Conservative government in office in 1913.

That is not my point,
and the minister knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not finding any fault
with the government of that day; I think it was a pretty good trade agreement with Japan. In 1922 we imported from Japan $8,194,682 worth of goods, and we exported about $14,900,000 worth; in 1927 the respective figures were $11,000,000 and $30,000,000 odd. That is a pretty good kind of trade.

Commercial Treaties
I submit experience will prove not what my hon. friend has suggested, but that this trade will be of equal advantage to the Dominion.

Will the minister give us
the trade under the French treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In 1922 we imported from
France $13,482,005 worth of goods, and exported $8,248,000 odd; in 1927 the respective figures were approximately $23,000,000 and $15,000,000. I admit at once that in this case the balance of trade is against us.
Referring again to agricultural implements, mentioned by my hon. friend, I observe that our total exports to all countries for the fiscal year ending March, 1927, were about $17,000,000 in value, and our total imports about $18,000,000. But had my hon. friends thought for one moment they would not have brought up this question, particularly as to the increase in our importations, because the records show that this increase is represented mainly by farm tractors and tractor parts. My hon. friends did not treat that industry as kindly as we did the agricultural implement industry in 1924. In 1918 they put these tractors on the free list, but did not make any provision for our manufacturers to get their raw material on the same basis, with the result that they put the industry right out of business. To-day we are not manufacturing any farm tractors, and last year we imported $8,000,000 odd.

What we did in 1918 was in the nature of a war measure to increase the production of grain at less cost. The minister knows that very well. What has he done to alleviate the condition? Nothing.
Mr. STEWART (Edmonton);	Did the
government supported by the hon. gentleman do anything for the industry between 1918 and 1921?

We simply took off the
tariff.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
But you
did not put it on again.

When the Union government was in power it was well understood that no tariff changes would be made except in a few instances; that is, there was no general adjustment. If what we did was wrong, why did not the present minister make the necessary change? Has he done anything?

The minister has again
followed his old course of imputing to me an adverse reference to the Japanese treaty that I never made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

What I complain of is that by this omnibus measure we are embodying in the seven treaties dealt with the treaty with France and the treaty with Japan, without any adequate knowledge of what the effect will be. Then the minister told us we had no information. But after we have been debating this and the other treaties for two days, he produces for the first time a letter from our trade agent in Hamburg. That letter contained only a suggestion to the government that the time had come when we should enter into treaties with these countries. My complaint is that the minister has had since 1926, when the letter was received, until 1928, to prepare his precis of this whole business, which should have been laid on the table with these bills so we would know what the effect would be. I am not complaining of the officers of the department. I am complaining that the government of the day brings down measures without furnishing the information to enable us to judge their merits. I protest vigorously against passing these treaties. It may be that they will work out satisfactorily, but we are going blind at the present time. As I said on a previous occasion, neither the minister himself, nor any of his colleagues, nor any official of his department, is competent to say now what will be the effect of these treaties.
